scope_rationale: Proposes a novel approach to value individual passes during football games by computing the expected reward of the possession (sub)sequence before and after each pass, then aggregates per-player pass contributions per 90 minutes. This is squarely within action valuation / pass valuation.
model_name: Pass contributions via possession-subsequence expected reward (k-NN + DTW)
model_inputs: event type;event subtype;timestamp (half and time);team performing the event;player performing the event;start location (start_x, start_y);end location (end_x, end_y);possession sequence trajectories (interpolated x and y coordinates at one-second intervals);shot location, distance to center of goal, angle to goal posts (for the xG sub-model)
model_target: Difference between the expected reward (expected goals) of the possession subsequence after a pass and the expected reward of the possession subsequence before that pass
model_architecture: k-nearest-neighbors search over possession subsequences with Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) as distance function, accelerated by clustering subsequences by start/end pitch cells (7x4 grid of 15m x 17m cells -> 784 origin-destination clusters); expected reward labels come from an XGBoost expected-goals model (500 estimators, learning rate 0.01, max depth 5)
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) coordinates; clustering uses a 7-by-4 grid of 15m x 17m cells on a 105m x 68m pitch
model_temporal_horizon: until end of the possession (sub)sequence
data_leagues: English Premier League;Spanish LaLiga;German 1. Bundesliga;Italian Serie A;French Ligue Un;Belgian Pro League;Dutch Eredivisie
evaluation_metrics: logarithmic loss (for predicting game outcomes home win / draw / away win via Skellam distribution over Poisson team-goal models seeded by player ratings)
evaluation_baselines: pass accuracy;prior distribution over game outcomes (48.42% home win, 28.16% away win, 23.42% draw)
splits: Chronological match-level split: train = 2014/2015 and 2015/2016 seasons (4,253 games); validation = 2016/2017 season (2,404 games); test = 2017/2018 season (2,404 games). Evaluation predicts outcomes for 1,172 games in the top-five European leagues.

scope_rationale: Unique angle in the corpus: the paper does not propose a new core action-valuation model but instead conditions player action values on quantified mental pressure. It adopts the VAEP-style contribution rating from Decroos et al. as its 'contribution rating' (V(s_j) - V(s_i)) and adds two novel per-action metrics: a 'decision rating' (chosen action's expected contribution rating minus the expected contribution rating across all possible actions, predicted by a GBT) and an 'execution rating' (action outcome indicator minus predicted success probability). All three metrics are then aggregated across pressure strata (top 20% / middle 60% / bottom 20%) defined by a learned pressure model that combines a pre-game pressure score (Gradient Boosted Ranking Trees trained on 330 pairwise expert rankings) with an in-game pressure score derived from a Bayesian (PyMC3 ADVI) future-goals win-probability model. Captures the mental-pressure-adjusted action value design space.
model_name: Mental-Pressure-Adjusted Action Value (Contribution / Decision / Execution ratings stratified by Pressure(g, x_t) = Pressure_pre-game(g) + Pressure_in-game(x_t))
model_inputs: team ambition features (previous-season result clusters, transfer value of top-20 players, spending on loans, Football Manager reputation score);game importance via Elo-based simulation of remaining fixtures + Kendall-Stuart tau-c between each possible game result and each expected final league outcome;recent performance (points obtained and deviation from Elo-expected performance over last five games);game context (home/away, opponent rivalry from Football Manager data, match attendance, time since coach was appointed);in-game state features for scoring intensity: number of goals scored, goal difference, number of yellow and red cards, difference in Elo-ratings of the teams, average number of attacking passes in the previous 10 time frames, average percentage of duels won in the previous 10 time frames;action features for action-success classifier: action start and end locations, body part used, start and end locations of previous actions in the sequence (end location excluded for shots);game-state features for next-action contribution predictor: current location of the ball, start and end locations of the previous two actions, action types of the previous two actions, speed of the sequence (distance traveled and time covered over last two actions)
model_target: Three per-action quantities: (1) Contribution Rating CR(s_i, a_i, o_i) = V(s_j) - V(s_i); (2) Decision Rating DR(s_i, a_i) = ECR|s_i,a_i - ECR|s_i where ECR is the expected contribution rating; (3) Execution Rating ER(a_i, o_i) = [o_i+] - P(o_i+). Action values are then conditioned on per-situation mental Pressure(g, x_t), with Pressure_in-game(t) defined as the sum of the increase in win probability and the increase in tie probability if the team would score at time t, derived from independent Binomial future-goals distributions y_>t,home | theta_t,home ~ B(T-t, theta_t,home) and y_>t,away | theta_t,away ~ B(T-t, theta_t,away).
model_architecture: Pre-game pressure: Gradient Boosted Ranking Trees (max_depth: 6, n_estimators: 50) trained on pairwise expert rankings. In-game pressure / win probability: Bayesian temporal stochastic model with logit(theta_t,home) = alpha_t * x_t,home + beta + Ha and logit(theta_t,away) = alpha_t * x_t,away + beta, priors alpha_t ~ N(alpha_{t-1}, sigma^2), beta ~ N(0,10), Ha ~ N(0,10); inference via PyMC3 Auto-Differentiation Variational Inference (ADVI). Contribution rating V(s): inherited from Decroos et al. VAEP framework (22 action types). Action-success classifier (per action type): Gradient Boosted Trees. Next-action contribution predictor (used for ECR|s_i): Gradient Boosted Trees, two heads estimating P(g_{i+1}+ | s_i) and P(g_{i+1}- | s_i) combined as ECR|s_i = [P(g_{i+1}+ | s_i) - P(g_+ | s_{i-1})] - [P(g_{i+1}- | s_i) - P(g_- | s_{i-1})].
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) action start/end locations
model_temporal_horizon: match split into T=100 time frames; in-game pressure and win probability evaluated per time frame; contribution rating evaluated per action via V(s_j) - V(s_i) (single-action delta within VAEP framework)
data_provider: proprietary (SciSports; event data covering EPL, LaLiga, Bundesliga, Serie A, Ligue 1, Eredivisie, MLS)
data_leagues: English Premier League;Spanish LaLiga;German Bundesliga;Italian Serie A;French Ligue 1;Dutch Eredivisie;North-American Major League Soccer (MLS)
data_seasons: 2014/2015 (EPL only, for long-term evolution);2015/2016 (EPL only, for long-term evolution);2016/2017;2017/2018;2018/2019 (up to November 11th, 2018)
evaluation_metrics: agreement with annotators' pairwise rankings (73.91% vs 79.79% inter-expert agreement) for the pre-game pressure model;probability calibration deviation (within 2.5% typical, max 9.61%) for the in-game win probability model;Area Under the Precision Recall Curve (AUC-PR) per action type for the action-success classifier (Table A.1);probability calibration deviation (within 3%) for the combined action-success model (Figure A.2);Mean Squared Error (MSE) for next-action P(g_{i+1}+ | s_i) and P(g_{i+1}- | s_i) GBT models (Table A.2);Pearson correlation between average contribution per 90 in high-pressure situations and in last-quarter (fatigue) situations: 0.136
evaluation_baselines: base rate of action success per action type (for AUC-PR comparison in Table A.1);average next game state value of all actions starting in the same location (baseline MSE in Table A.2);inter-expert agreement of 79.79% (reference for the 73.91% ranker agreement)
splits: Pre-game pressure ranker: 330 pairwise rankings on 170 games for training; 483 pairwise ratings on 20 diverse games (relegation, rivalries, underperforming teams, end-of-season dead rubbers) for validation. In-game win probability: 4232 EPL/LaLiga/Bundesliga games (2014/15-2017/18), 70-30 train-test split that respects the temporal ordering of games. Action-success classifier: trained on 2014/15 and 2015/16 of EPL, LaLiga, Bundesliga, Serie A, Ligue 1, Eredivisie and Belgian first division (2,430 games, 2.96M actions); validated on 2016/17 of the same leagues (2,404 games, 2.92M actions). Next-action contribution rating GBTs use the same datasets as Appendix A.3.

limitations: Pre-game pressure has no ground-truth label, so the model can only be evaluated against pairwise expert rankings; the learned ranker reached 73.91% agreement vs 79.79% inter-expert agreement, indicating residual disagreement that the model cannot resolve.;Because event data is used, the precise locations of off-ball players on the pitch are unknown, so the expected contribution rating across all possible actions in a state must be estimated indirectly by predicting the next action's contribution rating from the current game state.;For action types where the end location might leak information about success (e.g. shots), the end-location feature is excluded from the action-success classifier, limiting the features available for those actions.;Aggregation of execution ratings across different action types is explicitly avoided because the distributions differ (e.g. shots are typically less likely to succeed than passes), restricting how the execution metric can be summarised per player.;Use-case analyses require players to have played at least 900 minutes including at least 180 minutes in both high- and low-pressure situations, which excludes many players from comparison.;For Olivier Giroud the authors include data from his Arsenal period because there were not enough high-pressure moments at Chelsea, a data-availability caveat the authors flag explicitly.

scope_rationale: Introduces ECOM (Expected Contribution to the Outcome of the Match), a pass-valuation metric that measures players' involvement in creating goal-scoring chances by valuing the effectiveness of their passes via distance-weighted k-nearest-neighbors search over historical passes.
model_name: ECOM (Expected Contribution to the Outcome of the Match)
model_inputs: pass start (x,y) location;pass end (x,y) location;pass length;ball location 5 s prior to the pass;ball location 10 s prior to the pass;ball location 15 s prior to the pass;possession sequence membership;expected-goals label of possession sequence outcome
model_target: Expected added reward of a pass V(p_i) = V_e(p_i) - V_s(p_i), where the reward of a possession sequence is the expected-goals value of any goal attempt it leads to (0 otherwise).
model_architecture: Distance-weighted k-nearest-neighbors over historical passes using a learned six-component domain-specific distance function; passes pre-clustered by origin-destination pitch zones; possession-sequence labels produced by an XGBoost expected-goals model trained on shot location, distance to goal center, and angle to goal posts; weights for the distance function learned via Bayesian Optimization (UCB acquisition, 250 iterations, 10 initial weight sets).
model_spatial_resolution: Continuous (x,y) on a 105 m x 68 m standardized pitch; pass-clustering grid uses 15 m by 17 m cells; expected start reward V_s computed over a separate 15 m by 17 m grid.
model_temporal_horizon: Until end of current possession sequence (label is the expected-goals value of the possession sequence's terminal goal attempt, if any).
data_leagues: English Premier League;Spanish Primera Division;German 1. Bundesliga;Italian Serie A;French Ligue 1;Belgian Pro League;Dutch Eredivisie
evaluation_metrics: AUC-ROC;logarithmic loss;mean absolute error (MAE) on market value
evaluation_baselines: QPass approximation;QPass approximation xG;Pass accuracy;Historical prior distribution
splits: Match-level chronological split: training set = 2014/2015 + 2015/2016 seasons (4253 matches); validation set = 2016/2017 season (2404 matches); test set = 2017/2018 season (2404 matches). 555 matches with missing/incomplete data (mostly Belgian Pro League and Dutch Eredivisie 2014/2015) were omitted. Match-outcome prediction experiments restricted to English Premier League matches.

a match yields on average 2.4 goals and 22.4 goal attempts.;Section 5.1.2 | The expected-goals model is an XGBoost classifier trained on 190,762 shots (after mirroring 95,381 training-set shots) using shot location coordinates, distance to goal center, and angle to the goal posts; with 100 estimators, maximum tree depth 4, and learning rate 0.1, the validation-set AUC-ROC is 0.763 on 53,617 shots.;Section 5.2.3 and Table 5 | The optimal distance-function weight set under the default 15 by 17 m clustering uses only the lengths of the passes and the ball location 5 s prior (weights set to one), with the other components set to zero; the origin and destination locations of the passes are already implicitly accounted for by the clustering step.;Abstract / Introduction | Passes constitute around 70% of all on-the-ball actions in soccer matches; in the present dataset 69% of the 10,846,885 on-the-ball player actions are passes.
limitations: No ground truth exists for the true value of a pass, so evaluation is performed indirectly by predicting future match outcomes.;Method values only passes; other action types (shots, dribbles, defensive actions, off-ball runs, set pieces, goalkeeper actions) are not assigned ECOM values.;Only event-stream data is used; the distance function does not incorporate spatio-temporal tracking data of all 22 players.;Computational cost of pairwise pass-similarity search at scale required a clustering pre-step (15 by 17 m origin-destination zones) to fit within 32 GB of memory; the 105 x 68 and 52.5 x 34 settings were excluded for memory reasons.;555 matches with missing or incomplete play-by-play data were omitted from the dataset (mostly 2014/2015 Belgian Pro League and Dutch Eredivisie).;Passes occurring during the first 15 s of each half are omitted because historical ball locations are unavailable.
open_questions: Incorporate spatio-temporal player tracking data into the distance function to better capture the circumstances under which each pass is performed.;Learn the optimal dimensions for the clustering grid cells from data.;Experiment with grid cells that vary in size depending on the distribution of passes over the pitch.

scope_rationale: Introduces Pass Shot Value (PSV) and Average Pass Shot Value (APSV), an early data-driven framework for valuing passes based on their association with shot opportunities, using model weights from a supervised shot-prediction classifier. Directly relevant to the action-valuation / pass-value lineage in the SAVANT corpus.
model_name: Pass Shot Value (PSV) / Average Pass Shot Value (APSV)
model_inputs: pass origin location (continuous-valued 18-dim zone-closeness vector);pass destination location (continuous-valued 18-dim zone-closeness vector);origin-destination outer-product features (flattened 18x18 matrix);possession-level aggregation (average of per-pass feature vectors)
model_target: Binary outcome of a possession: whether the possession (>= 3 completed passes) ends in a shot taken by the offensive team (y in {1, -1}).
model_architecture: L2-regularized linear Support Vector Machine (LIBLINEAR) with asymmetric (class-specific) cost parameters; per-pass value PSV(i,j) = w_i^o + w_j^d + w_ij^od derived from learned model weights.
model_spatial_resolution: 18-zone pitch grid (3 rows x 6 columns) with continuous closeness-weighted representation to the N=2 nearest zones
model_temporal_horizon: until end of possession
data_provider: unspecified hand-labeled event-data vendor (Opta is referenced contextually but not stated as the source)
evaluation_metrics: AUROC;F-score
splits: Chronological game-level split: first 80% of games as training, final 20% as holdout; 5-fold cross-validation on the training set with folds constructed at the game level so possessions in a single game are not split across folds.
key_claims: Section 5.1 (Classification Results); Figure 3 | The shot-prediction model has an AUROC of 0.79 and an F-score of 0.31 on the holdout set.;Section 5.1; Figure 1 | 6 of the top 10 most influential features for predicting whether a possession ends in a shot involve zone 14 (the 'critical zone' centered in the field in front of the penalty box).;Section 5.1; Figure 1 | Zone 17 (directly in front of the opposing team's goal) does not appear among the top 10 features.;Section 5.1; Figure 1 | Passes to zone 14 from zone 5 or zone 9 (long completed passes into zone 14) have negative model weights, while the top two features overall are passes between corner areas and zone 14.;Section 5.2 (paragraph after Table 3) | Among players in the 'offense' category, APSV correlates significantly with goals scored over the season (rho = 0.27, p < 0.05), even though goals and assists are not used in computing APSV.;Section 5.2 | APSV is computed only over players with more than 200 completed passes in the 2012-13 La Liga season, and only over passes occurring in possessions of 3 or more completed passes.;Section 5.2; Figure 4; Table 2 | APSV is almost always negative because most possessions do not end in a shot; offensive players like Cristian Tello, Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and the midfielder Mesut Ozil have a positive APSV.;Section 3.2; Equation 1 | The 18-zone field representation uses a continuous closeness-weighted vector r^l of length 18 with N=2 non-zero entries, normalized so that the L1-norm sums to 1.;Section 4.1 | Each pass is converted into a feature vector of length 360 (18 origin features + 18 destination features + 324 flattened origin-destination outer-product features); a possession's feature vector is the average over its completed passes.;Section 3.1; Table 1 | On average, each La Liga team attempted around 18,000 passes during the entire 2012-13 season; Barcelona made the most (30,283) and Levante the fewest (13,094).
limitations: The analysis does not incorporate temporal information such as duration of possession or time elapsed between passes; the authors note that adding such information would provide more situation-specific insights.;The work uses only event data; the authors state that player-tracking data would better allow investigation into strategic aspects of the game not directly involving the ball.;Features do not capture sequential information within a possession; the authors note that expanding to sequential features could give a more detailed understanding of how passing strategy relates to outcomes.;The model is trained on a single team-agnostic dataset; the authors note that team-specific models built from a team's own event data could provide better analysis of strategies most promising in their system.
open_questions: Extend the framework to defensive actions: use actions taken by players on defense to predict defensive outcomes and rank players by defensive ability.;Incorporate temporal information (e.g. duration of possession, time elapsed between passes) into the analysis.;Utilize player-tracking data as the source dataset to study off-ball strategic aspects of play.;Expand features to include sequential information within a possession.;Build team-specific models from individual teams' event-data collections.;Extend the methodology to other sports such as basketball, where passing performance is also primarily measured by assists.

scope_rationale: STARSS is an action valuation method for soccer that splits matches into phases, assigns phase ratings based on similarity (via DTW) to historical phases that end in a goal, and distributes those ratings across individual actions. It directly fits the action-valuation / possession-value literature.
model_name: STARSS (Spatio-Temporal Action Rating System for Soccer)
model_inputs: event stream of actions (type, timestamp, player, team, x-y location);end location for passes;outcome for shots (off target, on target, goal);x and y coordinates of the actions making up a phase
model_target: Phase rating = proportion of the k most similar historical phases (by spatial DTW distance) that end in a goal; distributed to individual actions via exponential-decay action weights
model_architecture: k-nearest-neighbors over phases using multivariate dynamic time warping (DTW) on (x,y) action sequences; phase rating distributed across actions using an exponential-decay weighting scheme with parameter lambda
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) coordinates of actions
model_temporal_horizon: until end of phase (uninterrupted sequence of actions by one team; new phase on possession switch or >10 seconds gap)
data_provider: unspecified (play-by-play event data; co-author affiliated with SciSports)
data_leagues: English Premier League;German Bundesliga;Spanish La Liga
evaluation_metrics: STARSS rating per 90 minutes;player share of team rating (%)
evaluation_baselines: goals and assists per 90 (traditional metrics);hand-crafted weighted-sum approaches (e.g., WhoScored.com, Squawka.com)
splits: Chronological / temporal: for rating a match, only matches from the same league played before the date of that match are used to discover similar phases; no held-out test split with quantitative metrics reported.
key_claims: Section 2 (Dataset) | Dataset comprises 4253 matches, 7,569,802 game events, 110,290 shots, and 11,842 goals across the English Premier League, German Bundesliga, and Spanish La Liga for the 2012/2013 through 2015/2016 seasons.;Section 3.1 (Splitting matches into phases) | A new phase is started each time possession switches between teams or more than 10 seconds pass between consecutive actions.;Section 3.2 (Rating phases), Equations 1-2 | Phase rating is computed as the proportion of the k most similar historical phases (by multivariate DTW distance on (x,y) coordinates) that end in a goal; example: 13/100 similar phases ending in a goal yields rating 0.13.;Section 3.3 (Rating actions), Equations 3-5 | Action weights are computed via exponential decay (w_i = (1 - lambda) * w_{i+1}) with the last action weight set to 1, then normalised to sum to one across the phase, so the phase rating is fully distributed across its actions.;Section 4 (Methodology) | For all case studies, parameters are set to k = 100 and lambda = 0.25 based on domain knowledge and empirical analysis.;Table 1 | Alexis Sanchez tops the 2015/2016 Premier League ranking with a STARSS rating per 90 of 0.289 over 2446 minutes (0.478 goals per 90, 0.147 assists per 90).;Table 2 | Zlatko Junuzovic tops the 2015/2016 Bundesliga ranking with a STARSS rating per 90 of 0.271 (0.153 goals per 90, 0.383 assists per 90).;Table 3 | Lionel Messi tops the 2015/2016 La Liga ranking with a STARSS rating per 90 of 0.387 over 2728 minutes (0.759 goals per 90, 0.528 assists per 90).;Section 5.1 (and Table 2) | Five of the top-15 Bundesliga players play for FC Bayern Munich.;Figure 2 (Section 5.2) | In the El Clasico of 2 April 2016, Lionel Messi contributed 19% of FC Barcelona's team STARSS rating and Gareth Bale contributed 21% of Real Madrid's team STARSS rating.;Section 1 (Introduction) and Section 5.1 | Wingers and attacking midfielders tend to contribute more to a team's STARSS rating than strikers.;Section 3.2 (Rating phases) | Unlike most existing approaches to rate phases in soccer (which only take phases that lead to a goal or shot into account), STARSS rewards teams/players for getting the ball into dangerous places even if the phase does not lead to a shot.

scope_rationale: Introduces VAEP (Valuing Actions by Estimating Probabilities), a framework for valuing any type of on-the-ball player action in soccer using event stream data, along with the SPADL representation language; central to the SAVANT corpus of action valuation methods.
model_name: VAEP (Valuing Actions by Estimating Probabilities)
model_inputs: SPADL features: action type (categorical);SPADL features: action result (categorical);SPADL features: body part (categorical);SPADL features: (x, y) coordinates of action start location;SPADL features: (x, y) coordinates of action end location;SPADL features: time elapsed since start of the game;Complex features: distance and angle to the goal for start and end locations;Complex features: distance covered during the action in x and y directions;Complex features: distance and elapsed time between consecutive actions;Complex features: whether the ball changed possession between consecutive actions;Game context features: number of goals scored by the team possessing the ball after the action;Game context features: number of goals scored by the defending team after the action;Game context features: goal difference after the action;Previous three actions [a_{i-2}, a_{i-1}, a_i] used to represent each game state
model_target: Two binary probabilistic classification problems: P_scores(S_i, x_i) = P(goal scored by team possessing ball in next k=10 actions | S_i) and P_concedes(S_i, x_i) = P(goal conceded by team possessing ball in next k=10 actions | S_i). VAEP value: V(a_i, x) = Delta P_scores(a_i, x) + (-Delta P_concedes(a_i, x)).
model_architecture: Gradient-boosted decision trees (CatBoost), chosen over Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost based on Brier score and ROC AUC comparison
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x, y)
model_temporal_horizon: next k=10 actions
data_leagues: English top division;Spanish top division;German top division;Italian top division;French top division;Dutch top division;Belgian top division
evaluation_metrics: Brier score;ROC AUC
evaluation_baselines: Logistic Regression;Random Forest;XGBoost;No features (predicts mean class probability);Location-only feature set;Action type-only feature set;Location + action type feature set;Goals per 90 minutes;Assists per 90 minutes;Goals + assists per 90 minutes
splits: Temporal/seasonal split (match-level): first model trained on 2012/2013-2015/2016 to produce outcomes for 2016/2017; second model trained on 2012/2013-2016/2017 to produce outcomes for 2017/2018. Only league games considered; friendlies, cup, and European games excluded.
key_claims: Section 2.2 and Appendix A.1 | The paper introduces SPADL, a language with 21 possible action types (including passes, crossed corners, dribbles, throw-ins, tackles, shots, penalty shots, clearances, keeper saves), up to four body parts, and up to six possible results.;Section 3.1, Equation 3 (Definition 1) | VAEP value of an action is defined as V(a_i, x) = Delta P_scores(a_i, x) + (-Delta P_concedes(a_i, x)).;Section 4.1 | The framework uses k=10 future actions as the temporal horizon for the scoring/conceding labels, chosen based on domain knowledge and preliminary experiments.;Section 4.2 | Each game state S_i is represented using only the previous three actions [a_{i-2}, a_{i-1}, a_i].;Section 5 and Appendix A.2 | The dataset contains 11,565 games played in the 2012/2013 through 2017/2018 seasons in the English, Spanish, German, Italian, French, Dutch, and Belgian top divisions, with each game containing approximately 1250 actions on average.;Appendix A.2, Figure 4 | The most frequent action types in the converted Wyscout data are passes (64.63%), dribbles (8.69%), and interceptions (5.01%).;Table 3 | CatBoost with all features achieves Brier score 0.01376 and ROC AUC 0.7693 on P_scores, and Brier 0.00547 / AUC 0.7313 on P_concedes; CatBoost performs best across all design choices.;Section 5.6.1, footnote 5 | Only 1.5% (0.5%) of all game states lead to a scored (conceded) goal in the data.;Section 5.6.2 and Table 3 | The full feature set outperforms baseline feature sets (no features; location only; action type only; location + action type) on both Brier score and ROC AUC for both P_scores and P_concedes.;Section 5.2 and Table 1 | The VAEP top-10 player ranking for the 2017/2018 English Premier League season features players (e.g., Kevin De Bruyne, Eden Hazard, Riyad Mahrez) who do not appear in traditional goals/90, assists/90, or goals+assists/90 top-10 lists; the combined market value of the VAEP top-10 (1,110 million euro) exceeds those of goals (862 million), assists (760 million), and goals+assists (947 million) top-10s.;Section 3.2, Equation 4 | Player ratings are computed per 90 minutes as rating(p) = (90/m) * sum_{a in A_p^T} V(a_i), where m is the number of minutes played by player p during time frame T.;Appendix A.3 | Experiments were run on a server with Ubuntu 16.04, 128GB RAM, and two Intel Xeon E5-2630 v4 @ 2.20GHz CPUs (max 20 cores / 40 threads).
limitations: The VAEP framework only values on-the-ball actions; defending is often more about preventing the opponent from gaining ball control by clever positioning and anticipation, which is not captured.;It is hard to accurately compare players across leagues because it is easier to perform highly valuable actions in minor leagues (e.g., French, Dutch, Belgian) than in tougher leagues (e.g., English and Spanish); young talents in minor leagues receive higher ratings than those in English and Spanish leagues.;It can be hard to accurately compare players across clubs in the same league, as it is generally easier to perform valuable actions in a top club with strong teammates than in a mid-table club with weaker teammates.;Building trust in the ratings is challenging because traditional scouts are unfamiliar with the way of rating soccer players.;The ratings are slightly less intuitive than traditional metrics such as goals per 90 minutes, which complicates the task for analytically less inclined scouts to understand precisely what the ratings measure.

scope_rationale: Paper learns a value function over multiplayer positionings (game states) from tracking data using deep reinforcement learning; this is an off-ball/state-valuation method directly relevant to the action/state valuation literature.
model_name: Deep RL player positioning value function (Dick & Brefeld)
model_inputs: x/y positions of all 22 players at 25 fps;x/y position of the ball;partial speeds (sx, sy) movement vectors of all players;ball movement vector;ball possession indicator (+1/-1) for which team has the ball;image-like 9-channel tensor representation (positions of left-to-right team, right-to-left team, ball; x,y speeds for each team; ball x,y speeds)
model_target: Value function V(s) = expected discounted return G(s_t) over an episode, where reward is 1 if the ball possession episode ends in a 'success action' (team carries ball into final 25 m of opponent half, or into 18 m area around opponent goal in alternative scenario) and 0 otherwise
model_architecture: Deep convolutional neural network: three convolutional layers with 32 kernels of size 6x6 and ReLU activations, followed by a fully connected layer of 256 nodes with ReLU, and a single output node V; trained with TD(lambda) (lambda-return) batch reinforcement learning
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) rasterised into a 9-channel image-like tensor of width x height pixels
model_temporal_horizon: until end of ball-possession episode (episode terminates when team loses ball, play stops, or a 'success action' is performed)
evaluation_metrics: AUC (area under the ROC curve);standard errors of AUC
evaluation_baselines: trivial baseline using ball's distance from the goal as a measure of dangerousness (AUC = 0.5 diagonal line)
splits: Leave-one-game-out (LOGO) cross-validation: train on four games, test on the remaining game; episodes are flipped in x and/or y during training for data augmentation
key_claims: Section 'Time-dependent AUC' and Figure 3 | Even 13 seconds before the end of a possession phase, the AUC is still strictly above 0.5, indicating the learned value function captures positioning information well beyond uninformed guessing.;Section 'Experimental setup' | The first success scenario (final 25 m) yields 380 successful episodes and 715 unsuccessful episodes with an overall of 11,045 states; the second scenario (18 m around opponent goal) yields 224 successful episodes and 866 unsuccessful episodes with 11,340 states.;Section 'Area-dependent AUC' and Figure 4 | Using only positional information performs worse than using all available information (positions + movement vectors), though the differences are not significant in Figure 3.;Section 'Training procedure' | Discount factor gamma = 0.95 and lambda = 0.7 (chosen via grid-search) were used; batch size of 30 episodes and the Adam optimizer; early stopping via LOGO cross-validation on the training set.;Figure 3 | Average AUC ranges from approximately 0.85 (3 seconds before end of episode) down to approximately 0.65 (15 seconds before end) for the Movements + 25 m success scenario.;Section 'Area-dependent AUC' and Figure 4 | The approach easily beats a trivial baseline using ball's distance from the goal as a measure of dangerousness, which would yield AUC = 0.5.;Conclusion | Authors claim this work constitutes the first purely data-driven approach to machines that read and understand games and thus bridges the gap toward computational tactics.
limitations: Experiments are based on only five games of topflight European soccer.;The second success measure (18 m around the goal) has a reduced number of positive training episodes and increased influence of chance on the outcomes, leading to comparable but noisier AUC results.;Authors are not focusing on learning optimal controllers (i.e., not modelling how players should behave optimally) but only how good real players' behaviour is.
open_questions: Correlations between the dangerousness metric and traditional performance indicators like playing speed, passing, or expansion of teams could be used to group historic episodes against an opponent.;Such groups could be used to automatically devise strategic insights for an opponent (e.g., indicating that counterattacks were more promising than slow play-making or that cross passes led to more dangerous situations) and implemented in the respective game plan.

scope_rationale: Presents a data-driven model that rates actions of players in soccer with respect to their contribution to ball possession phases, using a graph recurrent neural network (GRNN) over players and the ball to jointly predict trajectories and ball-possession success. Extends Dick and Brefeld (2019) from positioning to actions, and derives aggregate performance indicators for player comparison.
model_name: GRNN action/positioning rating model (Dick, Tavakol, Brefeld 2021)
model_inputs: Tracking data: xy positions of all 22 players and the ball at 25 frames per second;Velocity of each player and the ball (estimated from differences over the last 0.12 s);Team indicator: whether the player's team is currently in ball possession;Per-player indicator: whether the player currently has ball possession;Indicator whether the team plays in positive x-direction (or vice versa);Indicator whether the player is a goalkeeper;Event data (passes, shots, tackles, etc.) augmenting tracking data for episode/success annotation;Sequence of player and ball states S_T^{0:N} fed into the GRNN
model_target: Two jointly learned predictions: (i) movement prediction p^i(Delta x | t, S_T^i) modelled by an MDN over relative xy movements of each player, learned by minimising the negative log-likelihood of observed movements; and (ii) value function V(S_T^{0:N}) = phi_V(u_T), the expected discounted future reward of a ball possession phase, where reward R(S_T^{0:N}) in {-1, 0, +1} is +1 if the team in positive x-direction completes their ball possession by entering the dangerous area while in ball possession, -1 if the opposing team does so, and 0 otherwise; trained with the lambda-return algorithm.
model_architecture: Graph recurrent neural network (GRNN) over a fully connected graph of all 22 players and the ball; two graph layers (GL) with GRU width 1024; attention functions alpha^type, alpha^v and function f_v have a single hidden layer of 512 units; input feature function phi_I has layers of sizes 128 and 256; Mixture Density Network (MDN) head with K=6 Gaussian components (means mu_k and variances sigma_k via two-layer MLPs of 512 units, ReLU and linear/exponential outputs respectively); value head phi_V is a two-layer MLP with 512 units and linear output. Implemented in TensorFlow.
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x, y) from tracking data; evaluation/visualisation also bins the pitch into areas (e.g., 6 m x 6 m cells in Figure 2)
model_temporal_horizon: until the end of the current ball possession phase (discounted future reward with gamma in (0,1)); episodes have average length 10.6 s
evaluation_metrics: ROC AUC (overall and per pitch area);L2 distance between observed and simulated player trajectories (with SE and Cohen's d, 95% CI);Mean difference in V between observed and simulated possessions (x 10^-4);Good dribbles per minute;Good passes per minute
evaluation_baselines: ConvNet value model of Dick and Brefeld (2019);Trajectory prediction model of Yeh et al. (2019)
splits: 5-fold cross-validation over the 54 matches; results reported as averages with SE error bars.
key_claims: Section 3 and Section 4 | A ball possession phase is considered successful if the team carries the ball into an area that extends 2 m outside the penalty box of the opponent (the 'dangerous zone'); this signal appears 1,879 times in the data and serves as a proxy for success.;Section 2 and Section 4 | The model is learned and evaluated on 54 Bundesliga matches from the 2017/18 season, with ball and player positions captured at 25 frames per second, augmented with event data on passes, shots, tackles, etc.;Section 3 | During the 2017/18 Bundesliga season, teams took on average 27 shots per game but only 2.79 were converted into goals; the data sample used here contains 148 goals and 1,450 shots (i.e., 1 goal out of 9.8 shots).;Section 4 | The data consists of 10,626 ball possession phases with an average length of 10.6 s; of those, 1,879 phases possess a non-zero success signal.;Section 3 (Success paragraph) | Reward R(S_T^{0:N}) is +1 if the team playing in positive x-direction completes their ball possession (ball S_T^0 inside the dangerous area and team in possession), -1 if the team in the other direction completes successfully, and 0 otherwise; V(S_T^{0:N}) = E[sum_{t=0}^{T_E - T} gamma^t R(S_{T+t}^{0:N})] with gamma in (0,1), learned by lambda-return.;Section 4 | The architecture used consists of two graph layers with GRU width 1024 and attention functions with a single hidden layer of 512 units; the MDN uses K=6 Gaussian components with two-layer 512-unit MLPs for pi, mu_k, sigma_k; phi_V is a two-layer MLP with 512 units.;Section 4, footnote 4 | The model was implemented in TensorFlow and learning took about 5 h on an Nvidia V100 GPU.;Section 4.1 and Figure 2 (right) | AUC values comparing V as a predictor for true success per small pitch area never fall below 0.64, even well inside the attacking team's own half (center-line at 52.5 m).;Section 4.1 and Figure 4 (right) | On AUC of true outcomes vs learned value functions per ball-to-goal-line distance, the proposed GRNN model significantly outperforms the ConvNet baseline of Dick and Brefeld (2019).;Section 4.2 and Table 1 | For trajectory prediction, the proposed model significantly outperforms the approach of Yeh et al. (2019) in all six role/whole-team settings under a paired t-test with p < 0.01; e.g., over the first 4 s, Whole Team distance is 1.91 +/- 0.07 m (this model) vs 2.16 +/- 0.07 m (Yeh et al., 2019), Cohen's d = -2.44 (95% CI -3.35 to -1.52).;Section 4.3 (Quantifying Player Performance) and Section 4.3.1 | A 'good dribble' is defined as one that increases V by at least 0.06 between the start and end of the dribble; analogously, a 'good pass' increases V by at least 0.06 between the time of the pass and the reception; dribble and pass effectiveness scores are aggregated per player among those who played in at least two full games.;Tables 2 and 3 | Top players by Good Dribbles per Minute (Table 2) include Kingsley Coman (0.078), T. Ito (0.063), A. Rebic (0.059), Jadon Sancho (0.053), A. Robben (0.053); top players by Good Passes per Minute (Table 3) include Jadon Sancho (0.058), Thiago (0.054), L. Rupp (0.054), K. Demirbay (0.050).;Table 4 | Top pass receivers by Good Passes per Minute (Table 4) include Breel Embolo (0.058), R. Lewandowski (0.057), A. Kramaric (0.056), James Rodriguez (0.054).;Section 4.3 and Table 5 | Mean differences in V (x 10^-4) between simulated and observed defending-team trajectories are small (~10^-4); during successful possessions, midfielders, wingers and attackers have a stronger negative influence on the outcome than defenders (e.g., Midfield: 1.0; Striker: 0.8; Winger: 1.0; Defense: 0.4).
limitations: The data only contains coordinates of players; their pose is ignored, so it is not always clear whether players are standing or lying, walking forward or backward.;A player who loses the ball due to a tackle may be physically pushed to the ground (without being fouled) and thus not able to track back immediately; this fact is unknown to the model.;Due to the conceptual approach, the model provides the same solution for all players in the same situation; it is not personalized and does not remember players across games or take a player's in-game history into account.;The model is oblivious to the state of the player regarding mental and physical fatigue.;Personalization would require access to additional data sources (load monitoring, self-perception of fatigue, stress, hours of sleep, muscle pain).;The dataset consists of only 54 games, and several players simply do not have enough games in the dataset to qualify for the player rankings.;The model is trained to estimate whether a ball possession phase reaches the dangerous zone just outside the penalty box, so many strikers may not appear on the player lists just because they typically operate closer to the goal.;Many shots and goals originate from set pieces and are not suitable for use as an outcome of a ball possession phase; the authors instead use a 'dangerous zone' proxy.
open_questions: Incorporating additional 'orthogonal' physiological or psychological data via a player embedding layer or by extending the input function phi_I (Equation 6) to personalise the model.;Whether the value function and derived performance indicators can serve as the basis for retrieval systems that automatically find complex tactical situations (pressing, counter-attacks) in match databases.

scope_rationale: Introduces a soccer-specific Expected Possession Value (EPV) framework that estimates the instantaneous expected outcome of a possession frame by frame from full-resolution spatiotemporal tracking data, decomposing EPV into independently estimated pass, ball-drive, and shot sub-models; a foundational EPV-style method for the SAVANT corpus.
model_name: EPV (Expected Possession Value) framework for soccer
model_inputs: Full-resolution spatiotemporal optical tracking data (22 players + ball);Pitch control surfaces (from a recent statistical pitch-control model, ref [9]);Pitch influence surfaces;Spatiotemporal features for passes and ball-drives (positional, motion, contextual);Relative location features defined by the opponent's dynamic formation lines (first, second, third pressure lines obtained via spectral clustering of mean X coordinates of defending players in a fixed 2-second window with 3 clusters);Movement, distances, and angles between players and locations;Expert-guided handcrafted contextual features
model_target: Instantaneous expected possession value EPV(t) = E[X | T_t], a real number in [-1, 1] expressing the likelihood of the possession ending in a goal for the attacking team (+1) or a goal by the defending team (-1) after an immediate possession regain; decomposed as EPV(t) = E[X|A=rho]·P(A=rho) + E[X|A=zeta]·P(A=zeta) + E[X|A=delta]·P(A=delta) over pass (rho), shot (zeta), and ball-drive (delta) actions, with the pass component further decomposed into expected value of successful pass, expected value of turnover, and pass probability.
model_architecture: Decoupled / decomposed model with independently estimated component sub-models: pass and turnover probabilities estimated with logistic regression; action likelihood modeled by a convolutional neural network on top of pitch control and pitch influence surfaces; pass and ball-drive value expectations learned by carefully designed deep neural networks; shot/expected-goals component described as a variant of expected-goals models. All components calibrated for accuracy at the component level as well as at the joint EPV level.
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x, y) over full-resolution tracking; value surfaces evaluated for every possible destination location on the pitch; defensive pressure lines obtained by spectral clustering into 3 vertical groups (relative zones Z1–Z4)
model_temporal_horizon: until possession ends (expected outcome of the current possession, evaluated frame by frame; ball-drives discretised every quarter of a second for the decision-making analysis)
data_provider: STATS LLC (optical tracking, 2012-2013 Premier League season); Footvision (optical tracking, FC Barcelona matches in 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 La Liga seasons)
key_claims: Section 2 (An expected possession value (EPV) framework) | EPV is defined as a real number in the [-1, 1] range, expressing the likelihood of a possession ending in a goal for the attacking team (1) or a goal by the defending team (-1) after an immediate possession regain.;Section 2, Equation (1) | EPV is decomposed as EPV(t) = E[X|A=rho]·P(A=rho) + E[X|A=zeta]·P(A=zeta) + E[X|A=delta]·P(A=delta), where the three components are passes (rho), shots (zeta), and ball-drives (delta).;Section 2, Equation (2) and Figure 2 | The passing component is further decomposed as E[X|A=rho] = E[X|A=rho, O_rho=1]·P(A=rho, O_rho=1) + E[X|A=rho, O_rho=0]·P(A=rho, O_rho=0), separating expected value of successful pass, expected value of turnover, and the pass probability model.;Section 2 (paragraph after Figure 2) | Pass and turnover probabilities are estimated using logistic regression; action likelihood is modeled through a convolutional neural network on top of pitch control and pitch influence surfaces; pass and ball-drive value expectations are learned from a set of carefully designed deep neural networks.;Section 2 (last paragraph) | Models were fitted using optical tracking data provided by STATS LLC for the 2012-2013 Premier League season, as well as optical tracking data provided by Footvision for FC Barcelona matches in the 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 La Liga seasons.;Section 2 (paragraph after Figure 2) | All component models are carefully tuned and calibrated for accuracy at the component level as well as at the joint EPV level.;Section 3 (The role of context within the unpredictable sport) | Defensive formation lines are extracted by applying spectral clustering to mean X-coordinate positions of each defending team player in a fixed 2-second time window, with the number of clusters fixed to three, yielding first, second, and third pressure lines.;Section 4 (Value: The missing key to pass analysis) | Passing is the most frequent action in soccer, reaching over 800 passes per match on average.;Section 2 and Figure 1 | In a Real Madrid vs FC Barcelona possession example, at the start of the possession EPV reaches -0.09 due to high spatial pressure from the opponent; a subsequent back pass increases EPV considerably (up to 0.04) by providing better conditions to further the possession up the pitch.;Section 5.1 (Off-ball demands according to positions) | Off-ball value is computed every time a pass is taken and every 1 second of ball-drives, taking into consideration all 10 teammates in each case (not just the player receiving the pass).;Section 5.1 and Figure 8 | Defenders are positioned in locations with low expected loss of value and low expected gain of value; the distribution widens for midfielders to a [-0.1, 0.1] range of expected EPV added; forwards show a higher tendency to move towards locations of higher value.;Section 6 (Decision making analysis) | For the decision-making analysis, ball-drives are split into discrete actions every quarter of a second; the set of possible actions is discretised by selecting the best pass location for every teammate, the location of the player in the next second according to his velocity for the ball-drive component, and the event of shooting from the current location.;Section 6 (Decision making analysis) | In a possession example, Sergi Roberto's ball-drive starts from a current EPV of 0.04 with two passing options that would have increased EPV up to 0.082; intense pressure during the drive decreases EPV down to -0.11.;Section 6 (Decision making analysis) | The model is trained to obtain the expected result for every action on an average player of the Premier League and Spanish League (the data used for training), but does not have individual player information.
limitations: The tracking data lacks body orientation information, so the model cannot understand that certain passes are more difficult than they appear (e.g., a forward pass requiring significant body rotation).;The model is trained on an average player of the Premier League and Spanish League and does not incorporate individual player information; in particular, individualised effects for players such as Messi keeping the ball would likely change the expectation of ball-drive in those situations.
open_questions: Identification of possession plateaus — windows of time where the possession is stabilised without variation — and extraction of actions that produce the jump between one plateau and another.;Extension to derive a wide set of metrics from frame-by-frame EPV curves (e.g., actions that increase/decrease possession EPV above/below a threshold) filtered by action type, field location, opponent relative location, and other contextual variables.;Application to opponent scouting by identifying locations and situations where a player is more likely to be located to increase the likelihood of the possession ending in a goal.

scope_rationale: Paper develops a Deep Reinforcement Learning model to learn an action-value Q-function for evaluating all types of on-the-ball soccer actions from event data, and derives the Goal Impact Metric (GIM) player ranking. Directly within SAVANT's action-valuation scope.
model_name: Two-Tower Dynamic Play LSTM (TTDP-LSTM) with Goal Impact Metric (GIM)
model_inputs: Game Time Remaining;X Coordinate of ball;Y Coordinate of ball;Manpower Situation;Goal Differential;Action (one-hot);Action Outcome (success/failure);Velocity of ball;Event Duration;Angle between ball and goal;Home or Away Team;play history sequence (s_t, a_{t-1}, x_{t-1}, ..., x_0)
model_target: Q_team(s,a) = P(goal_team = 1 | s_t = s, a_t = a): probability that team (Home/Away/Neither) scores the next goal given current state and action
model_architecture: Two-tower stacked LSTM (one tower per home/away team); each tower is a two-layer LSTM with 256 hidden nodes plus an embedding layer and two hidden layers with 256 nodes; outputs normalized via softmax to produce Q_Home, Q_Away, Q_Neither; trained with on-policy Temporal Difference (Sarsa) and a dynamic-possession LSTM trace length (max 10 steps); Adam optimizer with initial learning rate 10E-04 (general) and 10E-05 (fine-tuning). Interpretability via CART mimic regression tree.
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) on adjusted [0,100] x [0,100] pitch
model_temporal_horizon: until end of current goal-scoring episode (next goal or end of game)
data_leagues: English Premier League;Dutch Eredivisie;EFL Championship;Italian Serie A;German Bundesliga;Spanish La Liga;French Ligue 1;German Bundesliga Zwei
evaluation_metrics: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between estimated and empirical scoring probabilities;Correlation with standard success measures (Goals, Assists, Shots per Game, Pass Success percentage, Key Passes per game, Yellow cards, Red cards);Round-by-round correlation with season totals (assists, goals);Paired t-test (significance test between player evaluation metrics)
evaluation_baselines: Plus-Minus (PM);Expected Goals (XG);Scoring Impact (SI) (Schulte et al. 2017a Markov model);VAEP (Decroos et al. 2019);M-GIM (merged single-tower variant of TTDP-LSTM);DP-LSTM (Liu and Schulte 2018, ice hockey)
splits: Not explicitly described as train/val/test splits; model is fit on the full 2017-2018 multi-league dataset (over 4.5M events) with fine-tuning on EFL Championship league-specific data. No explicit match-level holdout described.
key_claims: Section 6.2 and Table 4 | The trained TTDP-LSTM achieves average MAE below 0.1 for all bins of context features (Manpower, Goal Differential, Period), significantly outperforming the discrete-state Markov Model baseline.;Table 10 | GIM achieves the highest correlation with 4 out of 5 positive success measures (Goals 0.844, Assists 0.498, SpG 0.596, KeyP 0.562) over players in all 10 leagues; only GIM and M-GIM show negative correlations with yellow/red cards.;Table 11 | Fine-tuned FT-GIM achieves the highest correlations with Goals (0.736), Assists (0.585), SpG (0.569) and KeyP (0.592) for EFL Championship players, and the largest negative correlations with Yellow (-0.110) and Red (-0.171) cards.;Section 9.1 (Significance Test) | Significance test (paired t-tests) rejects the null that GIM equals other player evaluation metrics with p-values 9.33E-2, 5.27E-281, 8.03*E-218, 4.82E-14 and 1.02E-118 for PlusMinus, XG, SI, VAEP and M-GIM respectively.;Section 7.3 (Proposition 1) and Appendix A | Proposition 1: For each player i, his Q-value-above-replacement equals his goal impact metric (QAAR^i(D) = GIM^i(D)), unifying the two fundamental approaches to player evaluation in an RL framework.;Table 3 | The dataset contains 4,679,354 events, 5,510 players, 2,976 games, 164 teams across 10 European leagues in the 2017-18 season.;Section 8.1 and Table 7 | Top-ranked player by GIM over the EFL Championship 2017-2018 season is Matej Vydra (GIM=18.017, 21 goals, 4 assists), who won the 2017-18 Golden Boot and was signed by Burnley the next season.;Section 6.1 (Spatial Projection) and Figure 5 | Spatial Q-value generalization shows that shot, pass, and cross Q-values increase with proximity to the opponent's goal, while defensive tackling Q-value increases with proximity to the team's own goal.;Section 5.2 (Training Settings) and Section 9.1 | TTDP-LSTM training uses Adam optimizer with initial general learning rate 10E-04 over 4.5M events (4,386,894 gradient steps) and fine-tuning learning rate 10E-05 on EFL Championship data (818,120 gradient steps).
limitations: Partial observability: the dataset records only positions and actions of the on-the-ball player; positions of off-ball players are unknown. The recurrent model partially compensates by inferring missing information from history, but performance is still limited by partial observability.;Big input data problem: the dataset has over 4M events including spatial/temporal features, making it difficult to use standard machine learning packages that fit entire data in memory; future work will explore online learning methods.;Convergence of on-policy TD with non-linear (neural) function approximators is not theoretically guaranteed; the authors mitigate by constraining look-ahead to the next goal and removing the discount factor.;Sparsity of goals in soccer makes reinforcement-learning style training challenging; the TD solution propagates scoring signals to previous events to address goal sparsity.
