scope_rationale: Introduces off-ball advantage (a probabilistic detector of when a player controls a valuable space such that passing to that player would substantially increase EPV) and effective value added (a long-term attribution of EPV to on-ball and off-ball actions), built on top of EPV pass-component values computed from tracking data. Also introduces a defensive area assignment via dynamic Voronoi over the opponent's expected formation to detect 'passes behind the back'. Directly relevant to action valuation, off-ball value, opponent scouting, and tactical pattern discovery in the SAVANT corpus.
model_name: Off-ball advantage detector + effective value added (with defensive-area passes-behind-the-back metric)
model_inputs: EPV before the execution of the pass;Distance and angle to the opponent's goal of the origin of the pass;Distance and angle to the opponent's goal of the destination of the pass;The potential value added by the pass, as the difference between the EPV expected at the destination of the pass and the current EPV just before the execution of the pass;Spatiotemporal tracking data (25 fps) and event data from FootoVision and Metrica Sports;Dynamic formation lines of the defending team computed via k-means clustering with k=3;Dynamic defensive formations built from mean vectors between players in 2-minute defending windows, resized and centroid-aligned to the current defensive block at each pass;Voronoi diagram over the expected (formation-derived) positions of defenders to assign defensive areas
model_target: Probability that a potential pass would become a short-term off-ball advantage (i.e. that the receiver's subsequent action ends with a higher possession value than at the start of the previous pass); effective value added per action as a fraction of the final possession EPV.
model_architecture: XGBoost binary probabilistic classifier (best hyperparameters: 2000 estimators, learning rate 0.01, max depth 4; random state 10; stratified shuffle split 70/30; 10-fold cross-validation). Auxiliary rule-based / geometric components: k-means (k=3) for dynamic formation lines; dynamic Voronoi diagram over defenders' expected positions for defensive area assignment; deterministic attribution rule that distributes the final possession EPV across on-ball actions proportionally to their (positive) value added (effective value added).
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x, y) from tracking; defensive zones derived from a Voronoi tessellation over the defenders' expected positions; defensive formations clustered into 3 lines via k-means
model_temporal_horizon: short-term for off-ball advantage (the receiver's immediately following action, with EPV evaluated when the pass arrives and at the end of the following action); until possession ends for effective value added; dynamic defensive formations built over 2-minute windows of defending
data_provider: FootoVision (event data) and Metrica Sports (spatiotemporal tracking data, 25 fps)
evaluation_metrics: ROC curve / ROC-AUC (curve shown in Figure 3; train log-loss 0.554, test log-loss 0.578 as labelled in the calibration legend);calibration plot (reliability curve, Figure 3)
splits: Stratified shuffle split into train/test with a 70/30 ratio, preserving the percentage of positive and negative samples; 10-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning; random state 10. Splits are at the example (pass) level rather than at the match level.
key_claims: Section 3 (Exploiting spaces of value) | Off-ball advantage is defined as a situation where a player is in a favorable disposition to receive a potential pass and, in case of receiving it, the player would likely improve the possession's value.;Section 3.1 (Methods) | The off-ball advantage detector is a probabilistic binary classifier whose features are: EPV before the execution of the pass; distance and angle to the opponent's goal of the origin and destination of the pass; and the potential value added by the pass (EPV expected at the destination minus current EPV just before the pass).;Section 3.1 (Methods) | The dataset consists of 65 matches played by FC Barcelona during the 2018-2019 and 2019-2020 seasons (both La Liga and UEFA Champions League), with event data and spatiotemporal tracking data provided by FootoVision and Metrica Sports at a frame rate of 25 fps; selecting all passes and the receiver's following action yields 46,780 examples; passes with negative potential value added are excluded.;Section 3.1 (Methods) | An XGBoost classifier was trained and tuned via 10-fold cross-validation; the best hyperparameters were 2000 estimators, learning rate 0.01 and depth 4; random state 10; stratified shuffle split into train and test sets at a 70/30 ratio, preserving the percentage of positive and negative samples.;Section 3.1 and Figure 3 | The model is correctly calibrated and the ROC curve achieved is shown in Figure 3; the figure legend labels XGBoost train log-loss 0.554 and XGBoost test log-loss 0.578.;Section 3.2 (Where do players create positional advantages?) | Three attack phases are defined for regular play (buildup, progression, finishing), and the three formation lines of each team are computed dynamically using the k-means clustering algorithm with a fixed value of k=3.;Section 3.2 and Figure 4 | Messi creates positional advantages between the middle and rear defensive lines mostly in the center of the block (even though his nominal position is right winger), while Coutinho produces somewhat fewer off-ball advantages mostly inside the defensive block but less centric — a typical trait of FC Barcelona wingers leaving the wings free for the full backs.;Section 4.1 (Methods) | Dynamic defending formations are built using the mean vectors between players in 2-minute windows when the team was defending; the formation is then resized to match the spread of defenders at the moment of the pass and its centroid aligned with the current centroid of the defensive block.;Section 4.1 (Methods) | A Voronoi diagram over the expected (formation-derived) defender positions assigns the area of the field to each player; the defender responsible for a pass is the one whose expected defensive location is closest to the position of the receiver. A 'pass behind the back' is detected when the receiver of the pass is closer to the goal than that defender.;Table 1 (Section 4.2) | Table 1 reports the number of passes received behind the back of midfielders when a center back was the closest player in front of the ball, for Team A (3 games, seasons 2018-2019 and 2019-2020) and Team B (4 games, season 2018-2019); Team A: LCB-LCM 14, LCB-RCM 7, RCB-LCM 9, RCB-RCM 13; Team B: LCB-DM 3, RCB-DM 10.;Section 5 (Attributing the long-term contribution) | Effective value added is defined as a percentage of the final EPV of the possession assigned to each on-ball action, calculated by dividing the value added to the EPV by that action by the sum of the equivalent values for all on-ball actions of the possession; actions with negative value added are discarded from the sum.;Section 5.1 and Figure 9 | Figure 9 reports two defensive stats normalized per 90 minutes for two UEFA Champions League group stage games (TOT-FCB 2018-2019 and INT-FCB 2019-2020): number of passes received behind the back per defender and mean effective value added of those passes; Barcelona generated their most dangerous attacks against Tottenham via key passes behind Trippier and Davies, whereas Inter generally maintained a more compact block, with Barella as the main exception (bypassed twice with high effective value added).
limitations: Deciding the threshold to discern true off-ball advantages from noise is not straightforward because EPV is non-linear and is affected by several dynamic factors (opponent pressure, player movements, pitch control).;Deciding who is responsible for a defensive error is a complex task; it is normally not a single action but an accumulation of events, so the passes-behind-the-back metric is intended to highlight trends across game sequences rather than to attribute a single error definitively.;A static defensive area approach would be expected to produce noisy and imprecise estimates due to the constant movement of the defensive block and role changes, motivating the dynamic formation-based assignment used here.

scope_rationale: The paper introduces DAxT (Defensive Action Expected Threat), a deep-learning model that values defensive actions (interceptions and tackles) in football event-data by predicting the xT of the passage of play that the defensive action stopped from happening. This is a canonical defensive-action valuation method.
model_name: Defensive Action Expected Threat (DAxT)
model_inputs: xT of preceding events in the sequence;x,y pitch coordinates of preceding events;fixed number of actions a=2 preceding the defensive action (per Experiment 1);SPADL-converted event-stream data (event type, location, time, player/team ID, result)
model_target: xT of the event that would have happened after the defensive action (i.e. f(e_n) = Theta(S_a)), where the predicted xT is then used as the value (I_V or T_V) of the interception or tackle
model_architecture: Multi Layer Perceptron (MLP) built with Keras; 3 dense hidden layers with 10 neurons each, ELU activation, MAE loss, Adadelta optimizer, trained for 50 epochs; inputs MinMax-scaled with Scikit-Learn's MinMaxScaler
model_spatial_resolution: 16x12 pitch grid (inherited from the xT model in Equation 2); raw (x,y) coordinates used as MLP inputs
model_temporal_horizon: next event after a sequence of a=2 preceding actions (i.e. predict xT of the event that would have followed the defensive action)
evaluation_metrics: Mean Absolute Error (MAE);Levene test (variance of residuals);Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test;Q-Q plot of normalized residuals;Pearson correlation coefficient (r) vs. actual values;Pearson correlation coefficient (r) vs. market value (Transfermarkt)
evaluation_baselines: baseline model predicting 0's (MAE = 0.0267);CIES Football Observatory and InStat Performance Index (2019 season) for ranking comparison
splits: Random 80-20 train/validation split on event-level instances (not by match); test set used in Experiment 3 for MAE evaluation.
key_claims: Section 1 (Introduction, contribution 2) | Using real-world data from 760 real-world football games from the past two seasons of the English Premier League (EPL), we train and test our model and find that we can accurately predict the impact of future events to an MAE of 0.015.;Section 5.3 (Experiment 3: Model Prediction) and footnote 8 | On the test set, the model returned an MAE loss of 0.016 (compared to a baseline model predicting 0's which would have a MAE of 0.0267).;Table 2 (Section 5.1) | a=2 was selected as the optimal number of actions in a passage of play; Training Loss = 0.0154, Validation Loss = 0.0153, Training Data = 802,046, Interceptions = 75,691, Tackles = 17,423.;Section 5.3 | Levene test returned a statistic value v = 1.209 and p-value p = 0.272 (>0.05), indicating training and testing residuals have the same variance.;Section 5.3 | Kolmogorov-Smirnov test returned v = 0.0174 and p = 0.8333 (>0.05), suggesting the two probability distributions are the same.;Section 5.3 (Q-Q plot discussion, Figure 3) | 96.1% of the data was between 0.05 and -0.05 in the residual visualization.;Section 5.3 | Pearson correlation test between model predictions and actual values resulted in r = 0.0985 with p-value less than 0.05.;Section 5.4 (Experiment 4: Valuing Defenders) and Figure 4 | Pearson correlation between defender score and market value (top 25 center backs, full backs and defensive midfielders) resulted in r = 0.533 and p = 3.37 x 10^-6.;Table 3 | Top 10 players with most cumulative I_V (interception value): James Tarkowski (1.605), Ben Mee (1.576), Nathan Ake (1.537), Lewis Dunk (1.508), Shane Duffy (1.473), Harry Maguire (1.457), Virgil van Dijk (1.447), Christopher Schindler (1.411), Jamal Lascelles (1.386), Steve Cook (1.357).;Table 4 | Top 10 players with most cumulative T_V (tackle value): Wilfred Ndidi (0.435), Christopher Schindler (0.4), Idrissa Gana Gueye (0.384), James Tarkowski (0.38), Cesar Azpilicueta (0.353), Nathan Ake (0.335), Luka Milivojevic (0.318), Aaron Wan-Bissaka (0.315), Ben Mee (0.292), Harry Maguire (0.286).;Tables 9 and 10 (Section 7.1) | Center Back ranking by defender score is topped by Virgil Van Dijk (37.901), Harry Maguire (36.3), Ben Mee (35.942), James Tarkowski (34.733), Shkodran Mustafi (34.636); 5 of the top 6 full backs (Table 10) have a low average of goals conceded/appearance with a high number of assists relative to the rest.;Equation 4 (Section 4.3 / start of Section 5) | The overall defender score is computed as Sc = ((I_V + T_V + CxT) / 3 + PxT) / 4, where I_V is interception value, T_V is tackle value, CxT is Clearance xT, and PxT is Pass xT; cumulative values per player are normalized to a 0-100 score.;Appendix A.1 (Data Conversion) | The dataset (StatsBomb event data for EPL 2017/18 and 2018/19, 760 games) was converted with SPADL; 75,691 interceptions and 17,423 tackles were available to value.
limitations: Some defensive actions will be valued less than they should be due to unique passages of plays; e.g., in a 3v1 counterattack situation in the middle of the pitch, even if the defender intercepts the ball, the model would not highly reward this action because similar passages of play are not usually of high threat (without taking into consideration the number of defenders behind the ball).;Future work for valuing defenders' contributions should be centered around the growing collection of tracking data to assess off-ball contributions and movement of defenders with models such as pitch control, evaluations of opposition marking, and stopping events before they have happened; however, due to the low availability of tracking data at this time, especially across different leagues, event-data approaches remain key.;DAxT depends on another player metric (xT), which becomes a problem in terms of interpretation: people need to understand Expected Threat first in order to comprehend the DAxT model.;Metrics such as Possession Adjusted Interceptions and True Tackle Win % are slightly more intuitive than DAxT ratings, complicating the task for analytically less inclined scouts to fully grasp the ratings.;Comparing DAxT to other baseline models remains difficult due to the lack of similar work; only one analogous paper [29] (Stockl et al.) uses tracking data to understand the defensive impact of players.
open_questions: Extend defensive valuation to leverage tracking data (pitch control, opposition marking, anticipating/intercepting events before they happen).;Develop methods that allow defensive actions to be valued from event-data in smarter ways, given the low availability of tracking data across leagues.;Normalize defensive action counts based on possession of the team to assess how much defending a player does relative to opportunity.

scope_rationale: Proposes a valuation method for on- and off-ball soccer players in a single holistic framework based on multi-agent deep reinforcement learning, estimating Q-values per player per action including off-ball movement directions.
model_name: Multi-agent deep RL with action supervision (on- and off-ball valuation)
model_inputs: 2D position coordinates of all 22 players;velocity data of all 22 players;2D position and velocity of the ball (23 x 2 x 2 dimensions, 92-dim state);one-hot action vector for each agent (14 actions);event labels (passing, shooting) from event data
model_target: Q-value (state-action value) of each of 14 actions for each of 10 attacking players at each frame, trained via SARSA TD-loss with terminal rewards (Goal: +1, EPV at terminal no-goal, Conceding: -1)
model_architecture: Recurrent neural network with single 64-dim GRU middle layer (ReLU), input 106 x 64 (state 92-dim + action 14-dim), output 64 x 14 Q-values; trained with SARSA TD loss + cross-entropy action-supervision loss (L_AS) + L1 regularization; Adam optimizer; lambda_1 = 0.01, lambda_2 = 0.1
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) 2D coordinates
model_temporal_horizon: until end of possession (attack sequence; min 50 frames, max T=300 frames equivalent to 30 seconds at 10 Hz)
data_provider: Data Stadium Inc. (event + tracking); J.League (season goals); Soccer-digest (expert ratings)
evaluation_metrics: TD loss (L_TD);action supervision loss (L_AS);Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rho);average Q-value (on-ball and off-ball)
evaluation_baselines: RL without action supervision (ablation);OBSO (Off-Ball Scoring Opportunities) [Spearman 2018];C-OBSO (Creating off-ball scoring opportunity) [Teranishi et al. 2022];season goals;expert ratings (Soccer-digest)
splits: Match/team-level: training and validation data = attack sequences from teams other than Yokohama F. Marinos (1669 train + 186 val); test data = Yokohama F. Marinos attack sequences (1236 series). Player valuation restricted to attacks within the attacking third.
key_claims: Section 3.1 | TD loss with action supervision (0.0034 +/- 0.0001) was smaller than that without supervision (0.0063 +/- 0.0004), while L_AS with supervision (3.9550 +/- 0.0005) was slightly larger than without supervision (3.9407 +/- 0.0005).;Section 3.1 | Average on-ball Q-values with supervision (0.0137 +/- 2.597 x 10^-4) were larger than those without supervision (0.0008 +/- 4.431 x 10^-5); average off-ball Q-values with supervision (0.0008 +/- 0.0035) were also larger than those without supervision (-7.123 +/- 0.0018).;Section 3.2, Fig. 3a | There was a high negative correlation (rho = -0.761) between season goals and average Q-values obtained by the proposed method, indicating the indicator tends to value defensive players who provided many passes.;Section 3.2, Fig. 3b | There was a moderate positive correlation between average on-ball and off-ball Q-values (rho = 0.618), suggesting the indicator tends to value similar play style between on- and off-ball situations.;Section 3.2, Fig. 4a | Low negative correlation between average rating by experts and average Q-value (rho = -0.218).;Section 3.2, Fig. 4b | Low negative correlation with average OBSO (rho = -0.305).;Section 3.2, Fig. 4c | No significant correlation with average C-OBSO (rho = 0.182, p > 0.05).;Section 1, Section 2.1 | The proposed method values on- and off-ball actions of multiple players (including those far from the ball) in a single holistic framework using multi-agent deep RL with discrete action space (14 actions) over continuous state space inspired by Google Research Football.;Section 1 | Off-ball players spend approximately 87 min of 90 min without the ball, motivating evaluation of off-ball contribution.
limitations: Since there is no true value for the Q-value, the performance of the model cannot be directly validated; only relationships with existing indicators were investigated.;Action supervision requires careful interpretation: too little supervision (lambda_1 << 0.01) yields insufficient learning of counterfactual action values, while too much (lambda_1 >> 0.01) may overfit to actual actions and not consider counterfactual actions.;Sample size for correlation analysis was small (N = 14 players who played at least 10 games), so rho was used as an effect size rather than p-values.;Tracking data for all players and timesteps in the J1 League are not publicly shared in such amounts, limiting reproducibility.;Goalkeeper was excluded; only 10 attacking-player RL agent models were constructed.;Player valuation was restricted to attacks within the attacking third for simplicity.;The model can only qualitatively investigate effectiveness in terms of modeling soccer agents, not quantitatively validate which model is best in a practical sense.
open_questions: Improve RL models for a more valid valuation of players.;Use more sophisticated rewards per action.;Combine with forward RL simulation.

scope_rationale: PlayeRank is a data-driven framework for multi-dimensional, role-aware evaluation and ranking of soccer players. It learns per-feature weights via a team-level classification task (LSVC predicting match outcome), then aggregates per-action contributions into a per-match player performance rating and role-based player rankings. Although it operates at the player/match level rather than the per-action probability level of VAEP/xT, it is an action-valuation framework: each event type/subtype/tag combination receives a weight that determines its contribution to player performance.
model_name: PlayeRank
model_inputs: soccer-logs (event data) from Wyscout;event type, subtype, and tags (e.g. pass cross/simple, accurate/not accurate, key pass, assist, opportunity);spatio-temporal coordinates (x,y) of each event used for role detection (player average position / centers of performance);match outcome (win vs non-win) used as supervisory signal for feature weighting;76 features per player-match obtained by counting events of a given (type, subtype, tag) combination
model_target: Per-match player performance rating r(u,m) = (1/R) * sum_i w_i * x_i, where w_i are feature weights learned by a Linear SVM classifier trained to predict team match outcome (win = 1, non-win = 0) from the team's aggregated feature vector.
model_architecture: Three-phase pipeline: (1) Learning phase - Linear Support Vector Classifier (LSVC, L2-SVM via scikit-learn svm.LinearSVC) trained on team-aggregated feature vectors to predict match outcome, yielding feature weights w; k-means clustering (k=8) over players' centers of performance (average event positions) with soft-clustering (k-silhouette, delta_s=0.1) for hybrid roles. (2) Rating phase - per-player-match rating computed as scalar product r(u,m) = (1/R) * sum_i w_i * x_i; goal-adjusted rating r*(u,m) = alpha * norm_goals + (1-alpha) * r(u,m); series aggregation via Exponential Weighted Moving Average (EWMA). (3) Ranking phase - role-based rankings R_1,...,R_z assigning a player to role R_i if assigned to it in at least x=40% of matches.
model_spatial_resolution: Continuous (x,y) positions on a normalised 0-100 pitch; centers of performance computed as per-match average event coordinates and clustered into 8 roles; spatial query module uses a tessellation into 100 equal-sized zones (one per ~m^2 region, with note that solutions scale to ~10^6 zones if desired).
model_temporal_horizon: Per-match rating aggregates all events of player u in match m; player rating over series of matches uses EWMA across matches.
data_leagues: Spanish first division;English first division;Italian first division;German first division;French first division;Portuguese first division;Turkish first division;Greek first division;Austrian first division;Swiss first division;Russian first division;Dutch first division;Argentinian first division;Brazilian first division;European Champions League;Europa League;World Cup 2018;European Cup 2016
data_seasons: last four seasons (as of 2018) for club competitions; 3 seasons for Champions League and Europa League; 1 season for European Cup 2016 and World Cup 2018
evaluation_metrics: AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) of the LSVC classifier (AUC = 0.89);F1 (F1 = 0.81);accuracy (= 0.82) on 5-fold cross-validation;Normalized Root-Mean-Square Error (NRMSE) between competition-specific and overall feature weights (avg ~6%);silhouette score (ss = 0.43) for k-means clustering of roles at k=8;majority concordance c_maj with three professional scouts (overall 68%);unanimous concordance c_una with scouts (overall 74%);Pearson correlation between player average rating and standard deviation across roles;Shannon-entropy-based versatility V(u,M)
evaluation_baselines: Flow Centrality (FC) by Duch et al. [12];Pass Shot Value (PSV) by Brooks et al. [6];majority-class baseline classifier (AUC=0.50, F1=0.48, accuracy=0.62);random baseline classifier weighted by class frequencies (AUC=0.50, F1=0.53, accuracy=0.53)
splits: 5-fold cross-validation for the LSVC feature-weighting classifier on 19,619 team-match examples (80% train / 20% test per fold). Splits are at the team-match level, not match level; the same match contributes two team-match rows (one per team) to the dataset, which could enable mild cross-team leakage within a match. Player rankings are evaluated against a survey of 211 player pairs judged by three Wyscout professional scouts.
key_claims: Abstract; Section 5; Figure 11 | PlayeRank achieves an improvement of up to 30% (relative) and 21% (absolute) with respect to the state-of-the-art Flow Centrality algorithm, and up to 16% (relative) and 13% (absolute) over PSV, on agreement with three professional Wyscout scouts.;Section 4.1, Table 1 | The dataset comprises 31,496,332 events across 19,619 matches and 21,361 distinct players (21K reported in text) over four seasons of 18 prominent soccer competitions.;Section 4.2; Appendix A, Table 7 | 76 features (Table 7) were extracted per player-match, defined by combinations of event type, subtype, and tag (e.g. pass-simple pass-accurate, foul-hand foul-red card).;Section 4.4 | The Linear SVC trained to predict match outcome from team performance vectors achieves AUC = 0.89, F1 = 0.81, accuracy = 0.82 on 5-fold cross-validation (vs AUC=0.50 for the majority-class and random baselines).;Section 4.3, Figure 4, Table 4 | The role detector (k-means with k=8 on centers of performance) yields the best silhouette score ss = 0.43; eight roles are identified: right fielder, central forward, central fielder, left fielder, left central back, right forward, right/central back, left forward.;Section 4.4, Figure 5 | Top-10 (most positive) feature weights are dominated by assist-related features (simple pass assist, cross assist, head pass assist, smart pass assist, high pass assist, touch assist, launch assist, key launch pass, accurate free kick, accurate shot); bottom-10 (most negative) are red-card and second-yellow fouls (hand, violent, protest, late, normal).;Section 4.4, Figure 6 | The average NRMSE between the overall feature weights w and competition-specific weights w^(j) is around 6%, and 16 out of 18 competitions have NRMSE < 7%; the two outliers are the European Cup 2016 (17%) and World Cup 2018 (20%) which are national-team competitions with fewer matches (51 and 64).;Section 4.5, Figure 7(a) | The distribution of player performance ratings is strongly peaked around mu = 0.39 with sigma = 0.05; ~94% of ratings lie within [mu-2sigma, mu+2sigma]; 'excellent' performances (r(u,m) > mu+2sigma) account for ~5% of the total and are unevenly distributed across players.;Section 4.5 | Only 11% of players achieve an excellent performance at least once; on average 9% of players reach excellence at least once; the maximum excellence rate is 21% for Neymar.;Section 5; Figure 11 | Validated on 211 player pairs (involving 202 distinct players) judged by three Wyscout professional scouts, PlayeRank achieves majority concordance c_maj = 68% and unanimous concordance c_una = 74% overall (vs 50% random baseline); concordance grows with ranking-distance gap, reaching c_maj=86% and c_una=91% when the gap is >=20.;Appendix C, Figure 14 | Inter-Rater Agreement Rate (IRAR) between two Wyscout operators tagging the same match is approximately 0.70 overall, indicating good agreement at both event and player level.
limitations: The framework excludes goalkeepers from the analysis because they have different game rules and would require a dedicated analysis.;Soccer-logs do not include off-ball actions, so important aspects of performance such as pressing and the ability to create spaces cannot be assessed in the current version of PlayeRank.;PlayeRank's role detection is based on a player's average position via k-means clustering, which is one of several possible approaches; more sophisticated role models (e.g. heatmap- or event-direction-based) are possible but were not adopted here.;There is no objective ground-truth definition of performance quality; the team-outcome supervision is used as a proxy.;There is no consolidated and widely accepted metric for measuring performance quality in all of its facets; the authors propose PlayeRank as a candidate.;Disagreement between PlayeRank and scouts is non-trivial when compared players are close in the ranking (ranking distance < 10), where unanimous scout agreement itself is only around 58%.
open_questions: Designing more sophisticated role-detection algorithms (e.g., AI-based methods proposed in the Soccer Data Challenge) and embedding them in PlayeRank.;Designing more sophisticated feature-weighting techniques to plug into the framework.;Extending PlayeRank to work with other data sources such as video tracking data and GPS data to describe spatio-temporal trajectories and out-of-possession actions.;Plugging new performance metrics into PlayeRank's architecture and evaluating its applicability to other team sports (basketball, hockey, rugby).;Investigating alternative ways to combine the spatial-query score s(u,Q) and player rating r-bar(u,M) for the player-retrieval application.;Designing role detectors that operate at the level of fractions of a match rather than the whole match.

scope_rationale: Paper introduces a supervised pass risk/reward valuation model on tracking + event data, valuing individual pass actions and applying the values to player and team ranking. Squarely in scope for action valuation (pass-value subset).
model_name: Pass Risk and Reward Model
model_inputs: ball X and Y location (origin and destination of pass);speed of the player in possession and the intended receiver;speed of the nearest defender toward the passer and the receiver;distance of nearest defender to the passer and receiver;nearest defender angle to the passing line;first time pass indicator;time from regaining possession;expected receiver membership (distance/min-distance x angle/min-angle);tactical game-state features (build-up, counter-attack, unstructured-play);formation features (high-block, medium-block, low-block; left/centre/right) via k-means clustering on aligned player and ball data;polar coordinates of all players relative to the goal being attacked;polar coordinates of defenders to the passer and receiver
model_target: Pass risk: probability (0-1) that the player will successfully execute the pass given the situation. Pass reward: probability that the pass made will result in a shot within the next 10 seconds.
model_architecture: Logistic regression classifier (chosen over non-linear black-box models for interpretability); features hand-crafted from tracking data; tactical and formation context added via tree-structured feature augmentation including k-means clustering on player XY positions
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) tracking at 10Hz
model_temporal_horizon: pass execution (risk) and next 10 seconds (reward)
evaluation_metrics: Log-Loss;RMSE
evaluation_baselines: Naive (average pass completion rate);Ball-Only (start and end position of pass);Tracking (micro features from tracking);Tracking + Tactics;Tracking + Formation
splits: Training set of 352,466 examples; parameters tuned on evaluation set of 114,257 examples; test set of 114,257 examples. For reward classifier: 7,427 positive and 136,180 negative training examples; 3,062 positive and 58,484 negative test examples. Split methodology (match-level vs event-level) not explicitly stated.

scope_rationale: Proposes a deep RL framework that goes beyond action valuation by deriving optimal team policies for ball-destination decisions, using tracking + event data modelled as a Markov Decision Process with policy-gradient optimisation.
model_name: Expected Possession Outcome (EPO) optimisation framework
model_inputs: (x,y) locations of all 22 players and the ball at 25 Hz;x and y velocity components of attacking and defending players;Euclidean distance of the ball to each pitch location;Euclidean distance of the defending team goal to each pitch location;angle between the ball and the goal for each pitch location;cosine of the angle between the ball and the goal for each pitch location;sine of the angle between the ball and the goal for each pitch location;ball destination location label;binary outcome of actions (success / turnover);11 input channels of size 105x68 representing the pitch
model_target: Selection probability surface (softmax over 105x68=7140 pitch zones for ball destination) and success probability surface (sigmoid per zone for possession retention); optimised via policy gradient to maximise Expected Possession Outcome (EPO) in (-1, +1)
model_architecture: Encoder-decoder convolutional policy network over 11 x 105 x 68 pitch channels with two output heads (softmax selection surface, sigmoid success surface) and a reconstruction decoder; off-policy policy-gradient fine-tuning
model_spatial_resolution: 105x68 pitch grid (7140 disjoint 1x1 m zones); continuous action space also used
model_temporal_horizon: until end of possession (discounted with gamma=0.99)
evaluation_metrics: log-loss;inference time (seconds);number of parameters;Expected Possession Outcome (EPO);EPO difference;improvement in expected goal difference per game
splits: Chronological 80%-10%-10% train/validation/test split respecting game order

scope_rationale: Proposes a deep reinforcement learning framework on event and tracking data of soccer matches to discover the most impactful actions at the interrupting point of a possession, providing optimal offensive and defensive action recommendations.
model_name: Deep RL policy-gradient framework for optimal offensive and defensive actions
model_inputs: 44-dimensional (x,y) normalized positions of the 22 players on the pitch from tracking data;angle to goal;distance to goal;time remaining;home/away indicator;action result (successful or unsuccessful);body id (head/body/foot);one-hot vector of actions A excluding the ending action
model_target: Categorical probability distribution over interrupting offensive actions (shot, foul, ball out) and defensive actions (foul, clearance, out, tackle, interception) at the end of a possession; trained via policy gradient to maximize expected goals for the offensive team and minimize the attacking team's scoring probability for the defensive team within the next 10 actions.
model_architecture: CNN-LSTM network (convolutional layers + max pooling + LSTM with 100 memory units + fully connected + softmax) trained with Policy Gradient (PG). A separate CNN-LSTM binary classifier estimates P(score within next 10 actions) used as the reward signal.
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) from tracking data; reported per pitch zone (left wing, left half-space, centre, right half-space, right wing) for aggregation
model_temporal_horizon: next 10 actions within a possession (possession length truncated/padded to 10)
data_leagues: 11 different national leagues of Portugal, Russia, Hungary, and Germany
evaluation_metrics: accuracy;categorical cross entropy loss;inference time;number of parameters;off-policy policy evaluation (OPE) with importance sampling;Chi-square distance (team effectiveness);mean reward (expected goal difference);Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of mean rewards
splits: Chronological split of attacking possessions: 80% train, 10% validation for hyperparameter tuning and model selection, 10% hold-out test.
key_claims: Section 'Dataset' (p. 3) | The dataset includes 98922 actions (including on-ball and defensive actions), 9462 possessions terminated by either one of the defensive actions of the opponent players or a shot, out, foul performed by the offensive players, and 329 goals.;Table 2 | CNN-LSTM achieves 80% accuracy and 0.55 loss with 1.39s inference time and 201,019 parameters, outperforming 3D-CNN (70%/0.65), LSTM (66%/0.71), and Autoencoder-LSTM (76%/0.65) on the test set.;Section 'Expected Goal Results' (p. 6) | The expected goal prediction binary classification model (CNN-LSTM) achieved 78% accuracy on the test set.;Section 'Optimization Results' (p. 7-8) | For the offensive team, the amount of expected goal difference before and after the interrupting action would be -0.1 following the actual policy, and 0.22 following the optimal policy on average of all episodes (0.32 improvement).;Section 'Optimization Results' — Offensive approach (p. 7) | In Centre, the optimal offensive policy proposes more shots and less fouls; modification in action frequencies results in 0.4 increase in mean rewards from -0.1 to 0.3 on average of all teams.;Section 'Optimization Results' — Offensive approach (p. 7) | In Half-Spaces, the optimal offensive policy suggests more fouls and more shots (long-distance shots); mean rewards increase 0.3 from -0.1 to 0.2.;Section 'Optimization Results' — Offensive approach (p. 7) | In Wings, the optimal offensive policy suggests increasing ball out actions and committing less fouls; mean rewards change from -0.1 to 0.15.;Section 'Optimization Results' — Defensive approach (p. 9) | For the defending team, the optimal policy can decrease the attacking team's expected goal difference by 0.2 following the actual interrupting defensive action, and 0.22 following optimal policy (0.02 improvement on average of all episodes).;Section 'Game State Representation' (p. 3) | Only 2.3% of the attacking possessions were truncated due to their length exceeding 10 actions.;Table 3 | Team A has the largest effectiveness in offensive actions (0.71), team E in defensive actions (0.78); team K and team I show the worst effectiveness in offensive (0.41) and defensive (0.39) actions, respectively.;Sections 'Game State Representation' and 'Training protocol and return' | Discount factor gamma is set to 0.99; possession length is truncated/padded to 10 actions; LSTM uses 100 memory units.
limitations: In this work the policies are optimized independently and assume that the behavior of the opponent team is not adapted to the optimal policy; multi-agent RL is left for future work.;Focus is on on-ball defensive actions; positioning decisions of teams are not considered.;Further information of the game context (e.g. pass height, length, angle, etc.), teams' and players' abilities and their specific strategies would significantly improve the results but are not included.
open_questions: Use multi-agent reinforcement learning to adapt the opponent teams with the optimal policy as well, which might decrease the amount of improvement in mean rewards reported in this paper.;Incorporate off-ball positioning decisions of teams in the optimization.;Include additional game-context attributes (pass height, length, angle) and team/player abilities and strategies.

scope_rationale: Foundational possession-value / action-valuation work that models soccer possessions as a Markov chain over discrete game states and weights each action by its incremental change in P(Goal). Direct conceptual predecessor of xT and VAEP.
model_name: Markov chain possession-value framework
model_inputs: (x,y) coordinates;event type;defensive pressure;defensive "state"
model_target: P(Goal) — probability that the current possession ends in a goal, computed by iterating the transition matrix until the probability of ending in an absorbing state converges (n=20)
model_architecture: Closed-form discrete-time Markov chain over 39 states (2 absorbing states + 7 set pieces + 30 states defined by zonal location and defensive state); transition matrix repeatedly multiplied until absorption probabilities converge
model_spatial_resolution: 7 zones (zone 0 = own half + center circle area; zones 1-6 partition the attacking half into a 3x2 grid around the penalty area)
model_temporal_horizon: until possession ends (absorbing states: Goal or End of Possession)
evaluation_metrics: R^2 (expected vs. actual goals);linear regression slope/intercept of expected vs. actual goals
splits: Monte Carlo bootstrapping with 1000 samples with replacement; 5-fold cross-validation (4 training folds, 1 evaluation fold). Split granularity (match vs. event) not specified in the slide deck.
key_claims: Slide 16 ('Validation – expected vs. actual') | Monte Carlo bootstrapping validation of expected vs. actual goals yields y = 0.9417x + 0.0134, R^2 = 0.99034.;Slide 16 ('Validation – expected vs. actual') | 5-fold cross-validation of expected vs. actual goals yields y = 0.9126x - 0.0832, R^2 = 0.97564.;Slide 18 ('Results – Set Pieces') | P(Goal) for set-piece states: Penalty 71.55%, Long Corner 2.39%, Short Corner 1.67%, Long Free Kick 1.67%, Shallow Throw-in 1.46%, Deep Throw-in 1.09%, Short Free Kick 1.08%.;Slide 6 ('States') | The state space comprises 39 total states: 2 absorbing states (Goal or End of Possession), 7 set pieces, and 30 states defined by zonal location and defensive state.;Slide 5 ('Dataset') | The dataset covers the English Premier League 2010/11 season with 123 matches, a minimum of 11 matches per team, and approximately 100,000 'deliberate' actions (about 800 actions per match).;Slide 14 ('Transition Matrices') | Iterating the transition matrix until the absorbing-state probabilities converge requires n=20 multiplications.;Slide 25 ('Top Performers') | Top individual offensive performers identified by the framework include Tim Cahill (0.286), Yaya Toure (0.283), and Cesc Fabregas (0.256).;Slide 26 ('Worst Performers') | Worst offensive performers include Darren Bent (-0.282), Peter Odemwingie (-0.195), and Gael Clichy (-0.176); many of the lowest contributors are goalkeepers, strikers, and defenders.;Slides 22-24 ('Not all passes are created equal', 'How does it work?', 'Another example') | Player offensive contribution is computed as the sum of incremental improvements in P(Goal) attributable to each of the player's actions in the possession chain (illustrated by worked examples giving e.g. Player 1: -0.08, Player 2: +0.11, Player 3: +0.72; and a penalty example with Player 1 (earner) +0.56 and Player 2 (missed taker) -0.71).;Slide 17 ('Comparing P(Goal)') | Comparing P(Goal) across teams reveals tactical patterns: as teams move lower down the table, scoring becomes harder; notable exceptions are Manchester City (3rd, underperforms offensively) and Wolves (17th, overperforms offensively).;Slide 26 ('Worst Performers') | Darren Bent's low ranking is explained by sample artefacts: only 1 of his 17 season goals was in the sample, and he had 19 opportunities with the ball at >10% chance of scoring (22% average) but converted only one.
limitations: Markov assumption: the current state is treated as independent of the previous state (it doesn't matter how the possession reached the current state — transition probabilities are the same regardless of history).;Hard to capture all information about game state; off-the-ball movement is just as important as on-the-ball movement but is not directly modelled.;Sparse data: not all possible combinations of game situations have been observed, and those that have been observed often have only a few data points.;Difficulty of dividing credit among players involved in a possession.
open_questions: Digging deeper into per-player data to identify specific situations (e.g. whether Clichy/Young/Kolarov are poor crossers) in which low-rated players underperform.

scope_rationale: Canonical introduction of Expected Threat (xT), a possession-value/action-valuation method that assigns a threat value to every pitch zone using a Markov-style model and then values on-ball actions (passes, dribbles) by the difference in xT between start and end locations.
model_name: Expected Threat (xT)
model_inputs: start location (x, y) of action discretised to a 16x12 pitch grid;end location (z, w) of action discretised to a 16x12 pitch grid;per-zone move probability m_{x,y};per-zone shoot probability s_{x,y};per-zone move transition matrix T_{x,y} over the 192 zones;per-zone goal probability g_{x,y} (simple xG)
model_target: xT_{x,y}: probability of scoring within the next n actions when in possession in zone (x, y); after iteration n the value represents the chance of scoring in the next n actions (post writes 'next 5 actions' when using 5 iterations).
model_architecture: Closed-form Markov-style recurrence xT_{x,y} = (s_{x,y} * g_{x,y}) + (m_{x,y} * sum_{z,w} T_{(x,y)->(z,w)} * xT_{z,w}), solved by fixed-point iteration starting from xT = 0 for all zones; 4-5 iterations sufficient for convergence.
model_spatial_resolution: 16x12 pitch grid (192 zones)
model_temporal_horizon: next n actions (n = number of iterations; ~5 in the post)
key_claims: Section 'Deriving xT' | xT can be formulated as the recurrence xT_{x,y} = (s_{x,y} * g_{x,y}) + (m_{x,y} * sum_{z=1..16} sum_{w=1..12} T_{(x,y)->(z,w)} * xT_{z,w}).;Section 'But wait, there's more...' | Starting from xT = 0 for all zones, iterating the formula converges in approximately 4-5 iterations.;Section 'But wait, there's more...' | At iteration 1 the formula collapses to xT_{x,y} = s_{x,y} * g_{x,y}, which is essentially an xG model.;Section 'But wait, there's more...' | xT after n iterations represents the probability of scoring within the next n actions.;Section 'Applying xT' | For the Arsenal vs Burnley example, Ozil's pass moves the ball from xT = 0.077 to xT = 0.158 (delta xT = 0.081); Kolasinac's pass moves it from xT = 0.158 to xT = 0.171 (delta xT = 0.013); xT therefore attributes 0.081 / (0.081 + 0.013) = 86% of the credit to Ozil and 14% to Kolasinac.;Section 'Top xT creators' (table) | Top xT creators in the 2017/18 Premier League season include Kevin De Bruyne (28.033), Cesc Fabregas (20.538), Jose Holebas (18.487), Alexis Sanchez (17.432), Riyad Mahrez (16.756), Granit Xhaka (15.834), Christian Eriksen (15.700), Cesar Azpilicueta (15.187), Xherdan Shaqiri (15.079), Ashley Young (14.988), David Silva (14.970), Jonjo Shelvey (14.728), Fernandinho (14.005), Paul Pogba (13.954), Mesut Ozil (13.914).;Section 'Visualizing per-team xT' | Per-team xT maps reveal that teams with similar shape (e.g. Manchester City and Spurs) can have very different magnitudes, indicating that City are more threatening given the ball in the same position due to a higher conversion rate of possessions into goals.;Section 'Deriving xT' (note) | The model is constructed over a 16x12 grid on the pitch, giving 192 zones.
limitations: Treating the action value as the xT difference between start and end zones makes the framework behave like a conservative force: dribbling path is irrelevant (path independence) and moving the ball in a loop yields zero reward, which is an inaccuracy tolerated for simplicity and due to the lack of tracking data.;The simplified model only considers successful moves (passes/dribbles completed without losing possession); unsuccessful attempts are excluded for tractability.;Only on-ball events (shoot or move) are modelled; defensive actions, off-ball runs, and goalkeeper actions are not valued.;Discretising start and end locations to grid cells loses precision; the author notes bilinear interpolation as a more precise alternative.
open_questions: Identifying and analyzing patterns of play such as counter-attacks by looking at how xT changes during the course of a possession sequence.;Assessing an individual player's decision-making relative to their team's xT profile (e.g. is the player making high-reward passing choices, or would shooting/dribbling be better in certain areas?).;Player scouting: predicting whether a player who has never played for the team will fit the system by checking whether his historical actions would lead to high xT gains for the new team.

scope_rationale: Constructs a probabilistic physics-based pitch-control model that values game states (off-ball scoring opportunities, OBSO) from spatiotemporal tracking data, directly addressing action/state valuation in soccer.
model_name: Off-Ball Scoring Opportunity (OBSO)
model_inputs: spatiotemporal player tracking data (positions and velocities of all players at 25 Hz);on-ball event data (match time, on-ball player, event type: pass, shot, goal, etc.);distance to goal
model_target: Probability that the attacking team will score with the next on-ball event given the instantaneous game state (P(G|D))
model_architecture: Probabilistic physics-based model decomposed into three conditional components: (1) Potential Pitch Control Field (PPCF) modeling per-player control probability via a differential equation using time-to-intercept (logistic CDF) and ball time-of-flight with aerodynamic drag; (2) Transition model as a 2D normal distribution over next on-ball location scaled by PPCF^alpha; (3) Score model as a monotonic function of distance to goal raised to a power beta. Parameters fit via Bayesian MAP with normally distributed priors.
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) on the pitch, integrated as probability densities; PPCF computed per-player per-location
model_temporal_horizon: next on-ball event
evaluation_metrics: Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC)
splits: 5 games reserved as training set for parameter fitting; remaining 53 games used as test set. Split is at match level.
key_claims: Table 2 | OBSO is more correlated with future goals than either shots or goals themselves are; per-player game-to-game PCC values are OBSO->OBSO 0.60, OBSO->shots 0.37, OBSO->goals 0.26, shots->shots 0.35, shots->goals 0.17, goals->goals 0.12.;Figure 8 | The average goals/match versus average opportunity/match across the 14 teams in the 53-game test set has a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.76.;Table 1 | MAP fits of the model parameters: s=0.54 sec (temporal uncertainty), lambda=3.99 Hz (control rate), kappa=1.72 (defensive advantage), sigma=23.9 m (transition spread), alpha=1.04 (PPCF exponent), beta=0.48 (score exponent).;Figure 3 | The standard deviation of the average displacement between subsequent on-ball touches is 14 m.;Figure 5 / Section 3.4 | For the example in Figure 5, the integrated magnitude of the OBSO is 1.1%.;Figure 7 / Section 5.2 | In the example match between Team I and Team D with a final score of 1-1, integrated scoring opportunities are 1.32 versus 1.47 despite Team I dramatically outshooting Team D.;Section 3.1.1 | Player acceleration and maximum speed are modeled with fixed values of 7 m/s^2 and 5 m/s respectively for the time-to-intercept calculation.;Section 3.1.3 / Equation 5 | The model assigns lambda_i = 0 to attacking players in an offside position, removing them from the control field.;Table 3 / Section 5.4 | The top 20 players ranked by mean OBSO/match are predominantly center forwards, but include a right winger, attacking midfielders, a center midfielder, a left winger, and notably a right back from Team A.
limitations: Score model ignores game state D apart from distance to goal; defensive positioning is only proxied through the PPCF rather than explicitly modeled in the score term.;Time-of-flight modeling choice (selecting the flight time that most closely matches the arrival time of the nearest attacking player) advantages successful passing to counteract limitations of the decision model.;The next on-ball event probability density lacks a preference for events that move the ball closer to the target goal, so opportunities that appear as clear scoring chances to a domain expert may be under-estimated.;The model does not directly account for the difficulty of crossing while running at speed, over-estimating chances in such scenarios and under-estimating chances for stationary, unpressured passers (footnote 7).;The opportunity for the player currently in possession is not considered in OBSO (footnote 8).;Small training set (5 games) and event-data synchronization issues motivate the Bayesian MAP approach with strong priors.;Event data timestamps carry stochastic noise on the order of three seconds, leading to moderate errors in player positions.;Future work is needed to refine the scoring model (Section 3.3) and the effect that defensive pressure and player speed have on the ability of a player to successfully deliver the ball to a teammate.
open_questions: Refine the scoring model to account for defensive pressure and player speed on pass completion.;Replace beta-based score adjustment with an improved scoring probability model in future iterations (footnote 6).;Incorporate a preference term for events that move the ball closer to the target goal in the transition density (footnote 5).;Allow per-player acceleration and maximum speed values to better model break-away situations (footnote 3).;Use the constituent control (PPCF) and transition models for additional soccer analyses beyond scoring.

scope_rationale: Critical conceptual and empirical comparison of two canonical action-valuation frameworks (xT and VAEP). The paper proposes no new method, but analyses design-choice differences, computes both rankings on StatsBomb Premier League 2018/2019 data, and contrasts the two methods on illustrative action types, top-25 player rankings, correlation with goals/assists, and split-half robustness.
model_name: xT vs VAEP (critical comparison)
model_inputs: ball location (zone on M x N pitch grid) for xT;previous three actions including action type, start/end location, distance and angle to goal for VAEP;action-context features such as distance covered and time elapsed between consecutive actions for VAEP;game-context features such as time remaining in the match and current score differential for VAEP
model_target: For xT: probability of scoring within the next i actions (zone value). For VAEP: P_score and P_concede within the next k actions, action value = delta P_score - delta P_concede.
model_architecture: xT: closed-form Markov chain solved iteratively over an M x N grid (16 x 12 in this paper, converged after 6 iterations). VAEP: two separate XGBoost gradient boosted tree classifiers (one for P_score, one for P_concede) trained on a feature representation of the last three actions plus game context.
model_spatial_resolution: 16 x 12 pitch grid (xT); continuous location features (VAEP)
model_temporal_horizon: xT: probability of scoring within the next i actions (iteratively expanded until convergence). VAEP: next k actions (fixed-length action window).
evaluation_metrics: Jaccard similarity coefficient between top-k rankings;Pearson correlation with goals per 90 minutes (g/90);Pearson correlation with assists per 90 minutes (a/90);Pearson correlation between split-half player ratings (robustness)
evaluation_baselines: xT (Singh, 2019);VAEP (Decroos et al., 2019);goals per 90 minutes;assists per 90 minutes
splits: Models trained on StatsBomb English Premier League 2017/2018 season and used to rate actions in the 2018/2019 season. Robustness analysis splits the data into two random disjoint subsets and computes Pearson correlation of per-player ratings across them.

scope_rationale: Paper proposes a Markov Decision Process framework learned from event-stream data to evaluate team shooting policies via counterfactual reasoning (probabilistic model checking), assigning location-based shot values and analyzing decision making (shoot vs. move). Directly relevant to action valuation and decision recommendation for shots.
model_name: MDP-based counterfactual shooting-decision framework (Van Roy et al. 2021)
model_inputs: ball location (state defined by current location of the ball);field partitioned into a 22-by-17 grid over the offensive half plus a single state for the defensive half (375 field states);three absorbing states: s_goal, s_no_goal, s_loss_possession;event-stream data of passes, dribbles and shots (StatsBomb);characteristics of actions and what happened prior to the actions (used by GBDT to predict intended end location of actions);StatsBomb xG values for individual shots (used to approximate the frequency-vs-efficiency trade-off)
model_target: Per-team MDP comprising: P(s, move_to(s'), s') (probability of successfully moving the ball from s to s'), P(s, shoot, s_goal) (location-based xG, i.e., probability of scoring from s), and policy pi(a|s); used to compute E[goals | pi] = sum_s E[shots in s | pi] * P(s, shoot, s_goal).
model_architecture: Closed-form Markov Decision Process learned per team from event data; Gradient Boosted Trees Ensembles used to predict intended end locations of move actions (to estimate transition probabilities); PRISM probabilistic model checker used to compute properties (e.g., probability of generating a better shot later) and STORM mentioned as an alternative; counterfactual policy alteration via proportional re-weighting of action probabilities; expected number of state visits computed from the MDP fundamental matrix N = (I - Q)^-1.
model_spatial_resolution: 22-by-17 grid over the offensive half (3.1m x 3.1m cells) plus a single state for the defensive half; 375 field states in total
model_temporal_horizon: until possession ends (absorbing states s_goal, s_no_goal, s_loss_possession); also aggregated to a full season via expected number of state visits
evaluation_metrics: average relative error between estimated and actual number of goals per team (11.38%);expected number of goals per season under a policy (E[goals | pi]);difference in xG between move-then-shoot scenarios and shooting immediately;probability of ever generating a better shot than the current one within the same possession
splits: Per-team MDPs learned from 17 teams that appeared in both the 2017/18 and 2018/19 EPL seasons (76 matches per team); no explicit train/test split reported. Accuracy assessed by comparing estimated number of goals scored (under the observed policy) to actual goals recorded in the data for each team.
key_claims: Section 1 (Introduction), page 2 | The seven high-volume long-distance shooters (Eriksen, Pogba, Kane, De Bruyne, Son, Hazard, Sigurdsson) converted 6.5% of their 416 long-distance shots across the 2017/18 and 2018/19 EPL; in the 4455 times these seven players touched the ball in the long-distance zone and did not shoot, their teams only ended up scoring a goal in 2.1% of these possessions.;Section 2.1 and Figure 2, page 4 | The MDP partitions the offensive half of the pitch into a 22-by-17 grid and uses a single state for the defensive half, yielding 375 field states (cells are 3.1m x 3.1m).;Section 2.2, page 5 | The MDPs are learned per team using StatsBomb event stream data from the 2017/18 and 2018/19 English Premier League, considering only the 17 teams that appeared in both seasons (76 matches per team).;Section 3.2.2 (Accuracy of estimating the number of goals), page 10 | The average relative error between the estimated number of goals scored according to the observed-policy analysis and the actual number of goals recorded for each team is 11.38%; for an average team scoring around 50 goals per season this corresponds to roughly six goals.;Section 4.2 and Figure 7, page 14 | The probability of ever generating a better shot in the same possession can be as low as 5% in some locations; on the edge of the box directly in front of goal it is only between 5% and 10%; in other locations (e.g., Manchester United's left side of attack) it can be around 20%.;Section 4.3 and Figure 8, page 15 | Uniformly increasing the frequency of long-distance shooting by 5%, 10%, or 20% increases the expected number of goals per season for most teams (e.g., Chelsea +0.3 / +0.5 / +1.0; Everton +0.2 / +0.4 / +0.8); some teams (Burnley, Liverpool, Newcastle United) see no gains or a slight decrease.;Section 4.4 and Figure 9, page 16 | A targeted increase in long-distance shooting (only from locations where shooting was deemed better than moving) yields expected-goal gains for all teams: shooting 10% more often yields about an additional half a goal per season, and 20% more often yields roughly an extra goal for most teams (e.g., Chelsea +1.6 at +20%).;Section 1 (Introduction, summary of findings), page 3 | Per-team analysis identifies specific long-distance zones where increasing shot frequency by 10-20% would likely lead to an increase of 0.5-1.5 goals in a season.;Section 4.4 and Figure 10, page 17 | Using data from the last ten EPL seasons (2010/11 to 2019/20), the figure shows that every goal scored during a season equates to roughly one point in the final table (fit Points = 0.956 x Goals scored + 2.451).
limitations: The 6.5% conversion figure for the seven long-distance shooters is likely an underestimate as rebounds (i.e., other chances created due to a shot from distance) are not taken into account (footnote 1, page 2).;Event stream data records the location where the ball went out of bounds but not the location it was intended to reach; hence the number of unsuccessful move actions from state s intended to reach state s' cannot be directly estimated from data and must be approximated using a Gradient Boosted Trees Ensemble (Section 2.2, page 6).;The MDP uses a coarse partitioning (22-by-17 in the offensive half, single state for the defensive half) chosen as a trade-off between expressiveness and data sparsity (Section 2.1, page 4).;Accurately modeling the frequency-versus-efficiency trade-off when altering the policy would be a complicated undertaking in its own right; the paper approximates it with a simpler adjustment based on the StatsBomb xG distribution within each state (Section 3.2.2, 'Estimating P'(s, shoot, s_goal) in pi'', pages 9-10).
open_questions: Extend the framework to other aspects of the game, e.g., analyzing whether a forward or a backward throw-in is more suitable in a specific situation, and how to effectively play out from the back (Section 6, Conclusions).;Further investigate the full potential of the framework (Section 6, Conclusions).

scope_rationale: Paper learns a Markov Decision Process model of soccer from event stream data to evaluate in-game decision making, including rating players' decision-making riskiness and analyzing shooting policies.
model_name: Markov model for soccer decision making (Van Roy et al. 2021)
model_inputs: event stream data;on-the-ball action type (pass, cross, dribble, shoot);start location of action;end location of action (observed);body part used to execute the pass;direction of the pass;start and end locations of the previous three actions in the sequence;success/failure flag;xG values of shots (used in counterfactual policy use case)
model_target: Per-state value V_pi(s) = probability of eventually scoring from state s under the team's policy; intermediate models predict P(action success) per state-action and pi(a|s) per state.
model_architecture: Hierarchical Bayesian model (Bernoulli/Categorical with Normal log-odds and Half-Normal variances, weakly-informative priors via Gaussian-smoothed counts) fit with PyMC3 ADVI; XGBoost gradient boosted trees ensembles for predicting intended end locations of failed passes and crosses; domain-knowledge post-processing; Bellman value iteration / fundamental matrix for derived quantities; PRISM probabilistic model checking for policy queries.
model_spatial_resolution: Two grids: (a) offensive grid with defensive half as one state and offensive half split into 3m x 3m zones; (b) regular grid of 12 x 16 cells
model_temporal_horizon: until end of possession (absorbing states: lost_possession, no_goal, goal)
evaluation_metrics: AUROC;Brier score;expected log pointwise predictive density (PSIS-LOO-CV);mean absolute error vs. empirically derived state values
evaluation_baselines: Baseline predicting prior distribution over observed end locations (for end-location prediction);Non-hierarchical (unpooled) Bayesian model with zero-mean Normal prior (sd=5.0) per team (for transition/policy models)
splits: 70-30 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation for XGBoost hyperparameter tuning on successful passes/crosses; Bayesian models evaluated using PSIS-LOO-CV; complete Markov model validated by comparing model-derived state values to empirically computed state values from raw data. Splits are event-level for end-location prediction (not match-level).
key_claims: Table 1 | With domain-knowledge post-processing, the pass intended-end-location model achieves AUROC 0.99 (+/- 0.00) and Brier 0.54 (+/- 0.02) on the offensive grid, and AUROC 0.99 (+/- 0.00) and Brier 0.69 (+/- 0.03) on the full regular grid, outperforming the XGBoost-only and prior-distribution baselines.;Table 1 | With domain-knowledge post-processing, the cross intended-end-location model achieves AUROC 0.95 (+/- 0.01) / Brier 0.77 (+/- 0.06) on the offensive grid and AUROC 0.95 (+/- 0.02) / Brier 0.58 (+/- 0.08) on the full regular grid.;Table 2 | Hierarchical Bayesian models outperform non-hierarchical (unpooled) versions on PSIS-LOO-CV expected log pointwise predictive density for both policy and transition probability models and for both state spaces (e.g., policy on offensive grid: -167.6 +/- 0.79 hierarchical vs -182.7 +/- 0.80 unpooled).;Section 5.3 | Mean absolute error between model-derived state values and empirically computed state values, averaged over the six teams, is 0.029 (+/- 0.01) using the offensive grid and 0.018 (+/- 0.01) using the full regular grid.;Figure 5; Section 6.2 | Counterfactual policy analysis indicates that shooting 20% more often from the identified good long-distance locations would add an estimated 2.5 additional goals per season for Chelsea, 1.6 for Huddersfield/Man City/Man Utd, 1.2 for Newcastle, and 0.7 for Burnley.;Tables 3 and 4; Section 6.3 | All players evaluated received a negative net risk rating, meaning all players perform more conservative actions than risky ones; least-risky top-10 is dominated by Manchester City players (e.g., Zinchenko -50.107), while most-risky top-10 is dominated by Burnley and Newcastle players (e.g., Jacob Murphy -7.697).;Figure 4; Section 6.1 | Team-specific good shooting locations exist outside the penalty box where shooting immediately yields higher chances of scoring than moving once prior to shooting; locations lie on both sides of the penalty arc for Chelsea, more on the left for Huddersfield, and more centrally for Manchester City.
limitations: Event stream data does not record the intended end location of failed actions, requiring predictive modeling and domain-knowledge post-processing to estimate them.;Data is sparse, particularly near the opponent's goal, motivating the hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage toward a global prior.;No ground truth model is available, making validation of the learned Markov model difficult; the authors must resort to indirect evaluation strategies.;Counterfactual policy changes cannot be implemented in real matches solely for evaluation purposes.;Event stream data contains no information about the location of off-the-ball players, limiting the amount of context that can be included in the model.

scope_rationale: The paper develops an automatic, quantitative metric (defensive anticipation) for evaluating off-the-ball defensive actions in soccer, using machine learning over player tracking data. This is squarely within the action-valuation / off-ball-action literature.
model_name: Defensive Anticipation Metric (P-score)
model_inputs: location of the player (2-dim);player velocity at time t-Delta (2-dim);location of the ball (2-dim);distance of the player to the ball (1-dim);distance of the player to offensive goal (1-dim);angle of the player to offensive goal (1-dim);location of the goalkeeper (2-dim);distance of the player to goalkeeper (1-dim);indicator for the player on offensive or defensive side of the field (1-dim);indicator for player belonging to the home or road team (1-dim);seconds remaining in the half of the game (1-dim);seconds remaining in the full game (1-dim);for each of the player's three nearest teammates: location (2-dim), velocity (2-dim), distance of the player to teammate (1-dim), distance of the ball to teammate (1-dim), relative angle of the teammate to the player of interest (1-dim);for each of the player's three nearest opponents: location (2-dim), velocity (2-dim), distance of the player to opponent (1-dim), distance of the ball to opponent (1-dim), expected possession value EPV of opponent (1-dim), relative angle of the opponent to the player of interest (1-dim)
model_target: Two-dimensional velocity vector (y1, y2) — directional components — of a defensive player in a given spatio-temporal situation; derived metric p compares observed vs predicted velocity to score defensive anticipation.
model_architecture: Two LightGBM gradient-boosted tree models (one per velocity component, x and y), trained over a 61-dimensional covariate vector built from tracking data. Per-instance score p is a closed-form projection (Eq. 1) of the observed velocity onto the predicted velocity direction; season-long P-score is the mean of p across instances scaled by 100% (Eq. 2).
model_spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y)
model_temporal_horizon: next instant (predict velocity at time t given state, with Delta = 0.5 seconds prior velocity covariate; analysis stepped every epsilon = 1 second)
data_provider: Shandong Luneng Taishan FC (CSL data provided by Daniel Stenz)
evaluation_metrics: mean absolute error of 0.319 m/sec in the x-coordinate velocity;mean absolute error of 0.398 m/sec in the y-coordinate velocity;correlation r ≈ 0.9 between predicted speed at time t and actual speed at time t-Delta (with Delta = 0.5 seconds);rank consistency of P-score across even vs odd weeks (Table 1: identical ranks for top-10 Shandong Luneng players);Pearson correlation between P-score and fouls = 0.60;Pearson correlation between P-score and successful tackles = 0.65;Pearson correlation between P-score and interceptions = 0.49;Leaguewise scatterplot correlation R = 0.32 (interceptions per game) and R = 0.29 (tackles won per game)
splits: 20-week season partitioned into training (even weeks 2,4,...,20) and test (odd weeks 1,3,...,19); leave-one-week-out cross validation used to select LightGBM tuning parameters. Split is by week rather than strictly by match; potential within-week leakage not discussed.
key_claims: Section 3.3 (Computational Overview) | Using roughly four million spatio-temporal instances, the LightGBM models predict the two-dimensional velocity vector of a defensive player; the fitted model provides a mean absolute error of 0.319 m/sec in the x-coordinate velocity and 0.398 m/sec in the y-coordinate velocity.;Section 3.3, Figure 1 | The tuning parameter Delta = 0.5 seconds was selected such that the correlation between predicted speed at time t and actual speed at time t-Delta is approximately r = 0.9 (Figure 1).;Section 2 (DATA) | The 2019 CSL dataset consists of 237 regular season matches (from a potential 240; 3 missing) across 16 teams, with tracking data recorded every 1/10th of a second (roughly one million rows per match across 7 variables).;Section 3.3 (Computational Overview) | The design matrix used for model training contained 3,770,289 rows and required just under 100 hours of computation on a laptop computer; LightGBM training itself required approximately 1.5 hours.;Section 4 (Results and Assessment) | Observations with predicted speed less than the threshold of 0.20 m/sec (0.72 km/hour) were removed from the metric; in the test dataset, 1.8% of observations were removed due to the threshold constraint.;Section 4.1 (Reliability), Table 1 | Reliability: for the 10 Shandong Luneng players with N > 10,000 instances in both even and odd weeks of 2019, the rankings produced by the defensive anticipation metric are identical across the two sets of weeks.;Section 4.2 (Validity), Table 2 | Validity: correlations between the P-score and season-long aggression statistics for the 10 Shandong Luneng players are 0.60 (fouls), 0.65 (successful tackles) and 0.49 (interceptions).;Section 4.2 (Validity), Figure 5 | League-wide, for all CSL players with at least 500 minutes played in 2019, scatterplots relate P to interceptions per game (R = 0.32) and tackles won per game (R = 0.29).;Section 4.2 (Validity), Figure 6 | Averaged across all CSL players in 10-minute intervals, P decreases as the match progresses, with a sharp drop after the 70th minute; this conforms to the common-sense expectation that defensive anticipation declines as players tire.;Section 4.2 (Validity) | Among CSL players with regular minutes, the two highest P-scores are Chang Feiya of Wuhan Zall (P = 5.71) and Yang Shiyuan of Shanghai SIPG (P = 5.33).;Section 4.2 (Validity), Figure 4 | Validity by playing position: among all 438 outfield CSL players (n = 79 wide midfielders, n = 77 wide defenders, n = 86 forwards, n = 110 central midfielders, n = 86 central defenders), there is little difference in P across playing positions; central midfielders have slightly larger values on average and forwards exhibit greater variability (Figure 4).
limitations: There is no gold standard for 'defensive anticipation' to validate against; the authors note that they 'do not know with certainty which players play with more and less defensive anticipation'.;The approach considers off-the-ball actions only for defensive players (i.e. when the player's team does not have possession); offensive off-ball movement is acknowledged as a more challenging future-research direction because there are multiple potential paths offensive players may choose.;Inferences are specific to the 2019 CSL season, although the methods are claimed to be applicable to any league with tracking data.;Three of the 240 potential regular-season matches are missing from the dataset.
open_questions: Investigating alternative predictive models beyond LightGBM for predicting average player movement.;Extending the framework to evaluate off-the-ball actions for players on the team in possession (offensive off-ball movement), which is harder because there are more viable options for offensive players.
